arXiv:2004.04905v7 [math.CO] 28 Jun 2023

Distributed Algorithms, the Lovász Local Lemma,
and Descriptive CombinatoricsThanks: This research was partially supported by the NSF grant DMS-2045412.

Anton Bernshteyn Address: School of Mathematics, Georgia Institute of Technology, Atlanta, GA, USA Email address: bahtoh@gatech.edu
Abstract.

In this paper we consider coloring problems on graphs and other combinatorial structures on standard Borel spaces. Our goal is to obtain sufficient conditions under which such colorings can be made well-behaved in the sense of topology or measure. To this end, we show that such well-behaved colorings can be produced using certain powerful techniques from finite combinatorics and computer science. First, we prove that efficient distributed coloring algorithms (on finite graphs) yield well-behaved colorings of Borel graphs of bounded degree; roughly speaking, deterministic algorithms produce Borel colorings, while randomized algorithms give measurable and Baire-measurable colorings. Second, we establish measurable and Baire-measurable versions of the Symmetric Lovász Local Lemma (under the assumption 𝗉​(𝖽+1)8⩽2−15\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)^{8}\leqslant 2^{-15}, which is stronger than the standard LLL assumption 𝗉⁡(𝖽+1)⩽e−1\mathsf{p}(\mathsf{d}+1)\leqslant e^{-1} but still sufficient for many applications). From these general results, we derive a number of consequences in descriptive combinatorics and ergodic theory.

1.  Introduction

A coloring, broadly construed, is a mapping that assigns to each element of a given structure one of a (typically finite) number of “colors” in a way that fulfills a prescribed set of constraints. The prototypical example is a proper kk-coloring of a graph GG, i.e., a mapping f:V⁡(G)→[k]f\colon V(G)\to[k] such that f⁡(x)≠f⁡(y)f(x)\neq f(y) whenever the vertices xx and yy are adjacent in GG. Classical problems in combinatorics often seek to identify sufficient conditions under which a coloring of a certain type exists.

In the last twenty or so years, a rich theory has emerged concerning the behavior of colorings and other combinatorial notions under additional regularity requirements. For instance, suppose that GG is a graph whose vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) is a standard probability space (e.g., the unit interval [0,1][0,1] with the usual Lebesgue measure). Does GG admit a proper kk-coloring f:V⁡(G)→[k]f\colon V(G)\to[k] that is measurable, meaning that f−1​(c)f^{-1}(c) is a measurable subset of V⁡(G)V(G) for every color cc? Questions of this type are the subject matter of descriptive combinatorics, which facilitates the fusion of ideas from combinatorics and descriptive set theory. For a state-of-the-art introduction to this area, see the survey [KM19] by Kechris and Marks.

Throughout this paper, we shall work under the assumption that the set of all available colors is countable (although there are interesting questions about uncountable colorings as well, see [KM19, §§3 and 6]). For concreteness, we can then assume that the colors form a subset of ℕ={0,1,2,…}{\mathbb{N}}=\{0,1,2,\ldots\}, so a coloring of a structure XX induces a partition X=X0⊔X1⊔X2⊔…X=X_{0}\sqcup X_{1}\sqcup X_{2}\sqcup\ldots of XX into countably many labeled pieces, called the color classes. Assuming that XX is a standard Borel space, we can then classify such colorings according to the regularity properties of their color classes. For instance, one can study Borel colorings, i.e., colorings in which every color class XiX_{i} is a Borel subset of XX. This notion turns out to be rather restrictive, so one often considers colorings in which every color class is not necessarily Borel but measurable with respect to some probability Borel measure μ\mu on XX or Baire-measurable with respect to some compatible Polish topology τ\tau on XX. On the other hand, sometimes one can aim for something even stronger than Borel; for instance, one might consider continuous colorings, in which every color class is a clopen set.

The goal of this paper is to adapt certain powerful techniques from finite combinatorics to the descriptive setting. Specifically, we establish the following two groups of results:

  1. (A)

    If a coloring problem on finite graphs can be solved by an efficient distributed algorithm, then on infinite graphs the same problem admits solutions with some regularity properties. (See Theorems 2.10, 2.13, 2.14, and 2.15 in §2.B for the precise statements.)

  2. (B)

    There is a measurable/Baire-measurable version of the Symmetric Lovász Local Lemma. (See Theorem 2.20 in §2.C for the precise statement.)

From these general facts, we derive a variety of new results in descriptive combinatorics, presented in §3. Here are just two examples (see §3 for the definitions of the terms used):

Theorem 1.1 (see Theorem 3.4).

There is Δ0∈ℕ\Delta_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property. Fix integers Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0} and cc. Let GG be a Borel graph of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta and let μ\mu be a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G). If c⩽Δ+1/4−5/2c\leqslant\sqrt{\Delta+1/4}-5/2, then the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    the chromatic number of GG is at most Δ−c\Delta-c;

  2. (ii)

    the μ\mu-measurable chromatic number of GG is at most Δ−c\Delta-c.

Theorem 1.2 (see Theorem 3.9).

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is Δ0∈ℕ\Delta_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property. Let GG be a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0} and let μ\mu be a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G). If GG contains no cycles of length 33 (resp. at most 44), then the μ\mu-measurable chromatic number of GG is at most (4+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ(4+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta (resp. (1+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ(1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta).

Theorem 1.1 was previously known only for c⩽0c\leqslant 0: the c<0c<0 case is due to Kechris, Solecki, and Todorcevic [KST99, Proposition 4.6] and the c=0c=0 case is due to Conley, Marks, and Tucker-Drob [CMT16]. The upper bound on cc in the statement of Theorem 1.1 is within 22 of best possible (see Proposition 3.6). The only previously known general upper bound on the measurable chromatic number of Borel graphs without 33-cycles, or even with no cycles at all, in terms of their maximum degree was Δ\Delta, which is implied by the result of Conley, Marks, and Tucker-Drob [CMT16]. Lyons and Nazarov [LN11] observed (see also [KM19, Theorem 5.46]) that there are acyclic Borel graphs with maximum degree Δ\Delta and measurable chromatic number at least (1/2+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ(1/2+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta, which means that the bounds in Theorem 1.2 are optimal up to a constant factor, even for acyclic graphs.

Let us now give some more details about bullet points (A) and (B). Distributed computing is an area of computer science that, among other things, investigates questions of the following form: Given a graph coloring problem, how far in the graph should an individual vertex be allowed to “see” in order to be able to compute its own color? This idea is formalized in the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model of distributed computation introduced by Linial [Lin92]. We describe this model here in a somewhat informal way; a precise definition, in the form needed for our purposes, is given in §2.A.

In the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model an nn-vertex graph GG abstracts a communication network where each vertex plays the role of a processor and edges represent communication links. The algorithm proceeds in rounds. During each round, the vertices first perform arbitrary local computations and then synchronously broadcast messages to all their neighbors. At the end, each vertex should output its own part of the global solution (i.e., its own color). There are no restrictions on the complexity of the local computations involved or on the length of the messages that the vertices send to each other, and the only measure of efficiency for such an algorithm is the number of communication rounds required.

We emphasize that in the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, every vertex is executing the same algorithm. This means that, to make this model nontrivial, the vertices must be given a way of breaking symmetry. There are two standard symmetry-breaking approaches, leading to the distinction between deterministic and randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms:

  • —

    In the deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, each vertex is assigned, as part of its input, a unique Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n)-bit identifier. The algorithm executed at each vertex is deterministic and must always output a correct solution to the problem, regardless of the specific assignment of the identifiers.

  • —

    In the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, each vertex may generate an arbitrarily long finite sequence of independent uniformly distributed random bits. The algorithm may fail to produce a correct solution to the problem, but the probability of failure must not exceed 1/n1/n.

We remark that deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms can be simulated in the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model: each vertex can simply generate a random sequence of ⌈3​log2​n⌉\lceil 3\log_{2}n\rceil bits and use it as an identifier—the probability that two identifiers generated in this way coincide is less than 1/n1/n.

Notice that in a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that runs on a graph GG for TT rounds, each vertex only has access to information in its radius-TT neighborhood. Conversely, every TT-round 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm can be transformed into one in which every vertex first collects all the information contained in its radius-TT neighborhood and then makes a decision, based on this information alone, about its color. This alternative way of thinking about 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms makes it clear how they measure the “locality” of graph coloring problems and is often more convenient to work with. (Indeed, this is the approach we shall use in §2.A to define 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms formally.) For further background on distributed coloring algorithms, see the book [BE13] by Barenboim and Elkin.

Now we can describe some of our results in group (A); for their precise statements, see §2.B. Fix Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}. We show that if a coloring problem can be solved by a deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that runs in o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) rounds on nn-vertex graphs of maximum degree Δ\Delta, then the same problem for Borel graphs of maximum degree Δ\Delta admits Borel solutions (see Theorem 2.10). Furthermore, under extra topological assumptions, “Borel” here may be replaced by “continuous” (see Theorem 2.13). Similarly, randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms that run in o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) rounds yield both measurable and Baire-measurable colorings (see Theorem 2.14), and “measurable” may be upgraded to “Borel” under additional assumptions on the growth rate of the underlying graph (see Theorem 2.15). These general facts enable one to prove new results in descriptive combinatorics simply by alluding to known distributed algorithms; for several such examples, see §3.

While the proofs of Theorems 2.10 and 2.13 (dealing with deterministic algorithms) are relatively straightforward, Theorem 2.14 (concerning randomized algorithms) is more involved. In particular, it relies on a novel measurable version of the Lovász Local Lemma that we establish in this paper, which brings us to bullet point (B).

The Lovász Local Lemma (the LLL for short) is a powerful tool in probabilistic combinatorics, introduced by Erdős and Lovász in the mid-1970s [EL75]. The LLL is mostly used to obtain existence results, and it is particularly well-suited for finding colorings that satisfy some “local” constraints. Roughly speaking, in order for the LLL to apply in this context, two requirements must be met: First, a random coloring must be “likely” to fulfill each individual constraint; second, the constraints must not interact with each other “too much.” The precise statement of the LLL requires a few technical definitions, so we postpone it until §2.C.1.

It has been a matter of interest to determine if the LLL can yield “constructive” conclusions (rather than pure existence results). The first such “constructive” version of the LLL was the algorithmic LLL due to Beck [Bec91]. Beck’s result requires somewhat stronger numerical assumptions than the ordinary LLL. This discrepancy has been eventually eliminated in the breakthrough work of Moser and Tardos [MT10]; for the long list of intermediate results, see the references in [MT10].

The Moser–Tardos method was later adapted to derive “constructive” analogs of the LLL in a variety of different contexts. For example, Rumyantsev and Shen [RS14] proved a computable version of the LLL. Here we are interested in the behavior of the LLL in the descriptive setting. When can the LLL be used to obtain Borel, measurable, or Baire-measurable colorings? Partial answers to this question have been given in [Ber19] by the present author and in [Csó+22] by Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros. The main results of both [Ber19] and [Csó+22] only apply under rather special circumstances: [Ber19, Theorem 6.6] is a measurable version of the LLL for structures induced by the Bernoulli shift actions Γ↷[0,1]Γ\Gamma\curvearrowright[0,1]^{\Gamma} of countable groups Γ\Gamma, while [Csó+22, Theorem 1.3] is a Borel LLL for coloring problems on graphs of subexponential growth.

In this paper we establish the first measurable/Baire-measurable version of the LLL that works without any such special restrictions (see Theorem 2.20). The drawback is that, as in the seminal algorithmic LLL of Beck, we require stronger numerical bounds than in the ordinary LLL. Nevertheless, just like Beck’s result, our measurable LLL is sufficient for many combinatorial applications. In particular, as mentioned above, it plays the central role in our proof that sublogarithmic randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms yield measurable/Baire-measurable colorings, and hence it lies at the heart of the measurable coloring results presented in §3. Of course, our measurable LLL can also be used without any reference to distributed algorithms. We give an example of such a direct application to a problem in ergodic theory in §3.E.

We remark that, while we use the measurable LLL to establish a relationship between randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms and measurable colorings, our proof of the measurable LLL itself relies on the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for the LLL that was recently developed by Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] and sharpened by Ghaffari, Harris, and Kuhn [GHK18]. Curiously, both the Fischer–Ghaffari algorithm and our proof of the measurable LLL do not invoke the Moser–Tardos method and instead go back essentially to the original ideas of Beck.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. We give the necessary definitions and state our main results precisely in §2. Next we present a variety of applications in §3. In §4, we explain how to turn distributed algorithms into colorings with regularity properties. Specifically, §4 contains the proofs of our results concerning deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms and reduces the results about randomized algorithms to the LLL. Finally, we prove our measurable LLL in §5.

2.  Main definitions and results

2.A.  Distributed algorithms for graph coloring problems

In this section we formally introduce the terminology pertaining to the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model of distributed computation. The nature of our main results requires us to be somewhat more pedantic with our definitions than is standard in the distributed algorithms literature. The reader who is already familiar with the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model is encouraged to only skim this section in order to familiarize herself with our notation and quickly move on to §2.B, where we connect 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms to Borel/measurable colorings.

2.A.1.  Graphs and structured graphs

Given a set AA, we write A<∞A^{<\infty} (resp. [A]<∞[A]^{<\infty}) to denote the set of all finite sequences (resp. finite sets) of elements of AA. Unless otherwise specified, by a “graph” we mean a simple undirected graph. Our graph-theoretic terminology and notation are standard; see, e.g., Diestel’s book [Die17]. In particular, the vertex and edge sets of a graph GG are denoted by V⁡(G)V(G) and E⁡(G)E(G) respectively. As usual, we write |G|≔|V⁡(G)||G|\coloneqq|V(G)| and ‖G‖≔|E⁡(G)|\|G\|\coloneqq|E(G)|. For U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G), the neighborhood of UU in GG (i.e., the set of all vertices with a neighbor in UU) is denoted by NG​(U)N_{G}(U). For a vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), we set NG​(x)≔NG​({x})N_{G}(x)\coloneqq N_{G}(\{x\}) and use degG⁡(x)≔|NG​(x)|\deg_{G}(x)\coloneqq|N_{G}(x)| to denote the degree of xx in GG. The maximum degree of GG is defined by Δ⁡(G)≔supx∈V⁡(G)degG⁡(x)\Delta(G)\coloneqq\sup_{x\in V(G)}\deg_{G}(x). A graph GG is said to be locally finite if degG⁡(x)<∞\deg_{G}(x)<\infty for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G). Throughout this paper we only work with locally finite graphs; in fact, we mostly focus on graph whose maximum degree is finite.

Sometimes one needs to consider graphs that support some additional structure. For instance, one might wish to work with directed graphs, weighted graphs, or graphs with a fixed coloring of the vertices. We capture this idea in the general notion of a “structured graph”:

Definition 2.1 (Structured graphs).

A structure map on a graph GG is a partial function σ:V​(G)<∞⇀ℕ\sigma\colon V(G)^{<\infty}\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} such that for some ℓ∈ℕ\ell\in{\mathbb{N}}, every tuple 𝒙∈dom⁡(σ)\bm{x}\in\mathrm{dom}(\sigma) is of length at most ℓ\ell. A structured graph is a pair 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma), where GG is a graph and σ\sigma is a structure map on GG.

In the above definition, we only use ℕ{\mathbb{N}} as the range of σ\sigma for convenience, as having the range of σ\sigma fixed once and for all will simplify some of the forthcoming definitions. In applications, any countable set could be used instead of ℕ{\mathbb{N}}, and indeed we shall often abuse terminology by referring to structured graphs whose structure maps range over different countable sets. For instance, we can view a graph GG equipped with a finite sequence σ1\sigma_{1}, …, σk\sigma_{k} of structure maps as a structured graph by replacing the tuple (σ1,…,σk)(\sigma_{1},\ldots,\sigma_{k}) with the single function

σ:⋃i=1kdom⁡(σi)→(ℕ∪{∗})k:𝒙↦(σ1​(𝒙),…,σk​(𝒙)),\sigma\colon\bigcup_{i=1}^{k}\mathrm{dom}(\sigma_{i})\to({\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\ast\})^{k}\colon\bm{x}\mapsto(\sigma_{1}(\bm{x}),\ldots,\sigma_{k}(\bm{x})),

where ∗\ast is a special symbol distinct from all the elements of ℕ{\mathbb{N}} and σi(𝒙)=∗\sigma_{i}(\bm{x})=\ast means that σi​(𝒙)\sigma_{i}(\bm{x}) is undefined. This is an acceptable construction since the set (ℕ∪{∗})k({\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\ast\})^{k} is countable. As a special case, given a structured graph 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma) and another structure map τ\tau on GG, we can interpret the pair (𝑮,τ)(\bm{G},\tau) as a new structured graph (with some “extra structure” added to that of 𝑮\bm{G}). This convention will become important when we formally define 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms.

Example 2.2 (Directed graphs).

A directed graph GG can naturally be viewed as a structured graph, since we can encode the directions of the edges of GG using the function V​(G)2→{0,1}V(G)^{2}\to\{0,1\} that sends a pair (x,y)(x,y) to 11 if and only if there is a directed edge from xx to yy in GG.

Example 2.3 (Multigraphs).

If the edges of a graph GG are allowed to have (finite) multiplicities, then we can view GG as a structured graph equipped with the function V​(G)2→ℕV(G)^{2}\to{\mathbb{N}} that assigns to each pair (x,y)(x,y) the multiplicity of the edge x​yxy.

Example 2.4 (List-coloring).

Sometimes, instead of assigning to each vertex of a graph GG a color from a fixed set, such as [k][k], one is required to pick a color for every x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) from its own list L⁡(x)L(x) of available colors (this is called the list-coloring problem; see [Die17, §5.4]). If every list L⁡(x)L(x) is a finite subset of ℕ{\mathbb{N}} (or of any other countable set), then the pair (G,L)(G,L) can be naturally viewed as a structured graph (since the set [ℕ]<∞[{\mathbb{N}}]^{<\infty} is countable).

We naturally extend all the standard graph-theoretic notation, such as VV, Δ\Delta, etc., to structured graphs; that is, for a structured graph 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma), we write V⁡(𝑮)≔V⁡(G)V(\bm{G})\coloneqq V(G), Δ⁡(𝑮)≔Δ⁡(G)\Delta(\bm{G})\coloneqq\Delta(G), etc.

Given a graph GG and a subset U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G), G⁡[U]G[U] denotes the subgraph of GG induced by UU, i.e., the graph with vertex set UU in which two vertices xx, y∈Uy\in U are adjacent if and only if they are adjacent in GG. Similarly, if 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma) is a structured graph and U⊆V⁡(G)U\subseteq V(G), then 𝑮⁡[U]\bm{G}[U] is the structured graph given by 𝑮⁡[U]≔(G⁡[U],σ|U<∞)\bm{G}[U]\coloneqq(G[U],{{\sigma}|{U^{<\infty}}}). (Here and in what follows we use the notation f|X{{f}|{X}} to indicate the restriction of a function ff onto the set X∩dom⁡(f)X\cap\mathrm{dom}(f).)

As usual, the distance distG​(x,y){\mathrm{dist}}_{G}(x,y) between two vertices xx, y∈V⁡(G)y\in V(G) is the smallest number of edges on a path in GG that starts at xx and ends at yy (if there is no such path, then distG​(x,y)≔∞{\mathrm{dist}}_{G}(x,y)\coloneqq\infty). For a vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) and a number R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, we define BG​(x,R)B_{G}(x,R) to be the ball of radius RR around xx in GG, i.e., the subgraph of GG induced by the set {y∈V⁡(G):distG​(x,y)⩽R}\{y\in V(G)\,:\,{\mathrm{dist}}_{G}(x,y)\leqslant R\}. The definition of B𝑮​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R) for structured graphs 𝑮\bm{G} is the same, mutatis mutandis.

We say that two structured graphs 𝑮1=(G1,σ1)\bm{G}_{1}=(G_{1},\sigma_{1}) and 𝑮2=(G2,σ2)\bm{G}_{2}=(G_{2},\sigma_{2}) are isomorphic if there is an isomorphism between their underlying graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2} that turns the function σ1\sigma_{1} into σ2\sigma_{2}. More formally, each function φ:V⁡(G1)→V⁡(G2)\varphi\colon V(G_{1})\to V(G_{2}) can be extended to a map V​(G1)<∞→V​(G2)<∞V(G_{1})^{<\infty}\to V(G_{2})^{<\infty} in the obvious way; namely, given a tuple 𝒙=(x1,…,xk)∈V​(G1)<∞\bm{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V(G_{1})^{<\infty}, define

φ⁡(𝒙)≔(φ⁡(x1),…,φ⁡(xk))∈V​(G2)<∞.\varphi(\bm{x})\,\coloneqq\,(\varphi(x_{1}),\ldots,\varphi(x_{k}))\,\in\,V(G_{2})^{<\infty}.

An isomorphism between 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1} and 𝑮2\bm{G}_{2} is a function φ:V⁡(G1)→V⁡(G2)\varphi\colon V(G_{1})\to V(G_{2}) such that:

  • —

    φ\varphi is an isomorphism of the graphs G1G_{1} and G2G_{2};

  • —

    dom⁡(σ2)=φ⁡(dom⁡(σ1))\mathrm{dom}(\sigma_{2})=\varphi(\mathrm{dom}(\sigma_{1})); and

  • —

    for all 𝒙∈dom⁡(σ1)\bm{x}\in\mathrm{dom}(\sigma_{1}), σ1​(𝒙)=σ2​(φ⁡(𝒙))\sigma_{1}(\bm{x})=\sigma_{2}(\varphi(\bm{x})).

We say that 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1} and 𝑮2\bm{G}_{2} are isomorphic, in symbols 𝑮1≅𝑮2\bm{G}_{1}\cong\bm{G}_{2}, if there is an isomorphism between 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1} and 𝑮2\bm{G}_{2}. The isomorphism class of a structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} is denoted by [𝑮][\bm{G}]. The set of all the isomorphism classes of finite structured graphs is denoted by 𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{FSG}. Notice that 𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{FSG} is a countable set (here we exploit the fact that the range of σ\sigma in Definition 2.1 is assumed to be the fixed set ℕ{\mathbb{N}}).

A rooted graph is a pair (G,x)(G,x), where GG is a graph and x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) is a distinguished vertex, called the root. Isomorphisms between rooted graphs are required to preserve the roots. One similarly defines rooted structured graphs (𝑮,x)(\bm{G},x). To simplify the notation, we denote the isomorphism class of a rooted structured graph (𝑮,x)(\bm{G},x) by [𝑮,x][\bm{G},x] (instead of [(𝑮,x)][(\bm{G},x)]). The set of all the isomorphism classes of finite rooted structured graphs is denoted by 𝖥𝖲𝖦∙\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}. Again, the set 𝖥𝖲𝖦∙\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet} is countable.

2.A.2.  𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms

Now we have enough notation to start defining the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model.

Definition 2.5 (𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms).

A 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm is a function 𝒜:𝖥𝖲𝖦∙→ℕ\mathcal{A}\colon\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\to{\mathbb{N}}. Given a locally finite structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} and a natural number T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, the output of 𝒜\mathcal{A} on G\bm{G} after TT rounds is the function 𝒜⁡(𝑮,T):V⁡(𝑮)→ℕ\mathcal{A}(\bm{G},T)\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} given by

𝒜⁡(𝑮,T)​(x)≔𝒜⁡([B𝑮​(x,T),x])for all ​x∈V⁡(𝑮).\mathcal{A}(\bm{G},T)(x)\,\coloneqq\,\mathcal{A}\left([B_{\bm{G}}(x,T),x]\right)\qquad\text{for all }x\in V(\bm{G}).

Note that since 𝑮\bm{G} is locally finite, B𝑮​(x,T)B_{\bm{G}}(x,T) is finite, so this definition makes sense.

Informally, Definition 2.5 says that a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} operates on a locally finite structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} as follows. Each vertex x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}) “sees” the isomorphism type of its radius-TT ball B𝑮​(x,T)B_{\bm{G}}(x,T), which is viewed as a structured graph rooted at xx. The algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} is then a “rule” that uses this information to output a “color” 𝒜​(𝑮,T)​(x)∈ℕ\mathcal{A}(\bm{G},T)(x)\in{\mathbb{N}}. The same comment as after Definition 2.1 applies here: instead of the set ℕ{\mathbb{N}} in Definition 2.5, any other countable set of possible outputs could be (and often is) used.

So far we have defined how 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms operate. Now we need to describe what problems they can solve. The problems we consider are sometimes called “locally checkable labeling problems” in the distributed computing literature (this term was introduced in the seminal work of Naor and Stockmeyer [NS95]). However, in order to stay closer to the terminology in descriptive combinatorics and in graph theory, we prefer to use the word “coloring” instead of “labeling.”

Recall that if 𝑮\bm{G} is a structured graph and f:V⁡(𝑮)⇀ℕf\colon V(\bm{G})\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} is a partial function (or, more generally, a structure map), then the pair (𝑮,f)(\bm{G},f) can be thought of as a structured graph in its own right, in which the function ff is “added” to the structure (see the comments after Definition 2.1). For brevity, we denote this structured graph by 𝑮f\bm{G}_{f}.

Definition 2.6 (Local coloring problems).

A local coloring problem (or a locally checkable labeling problem) is a pair Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}), where t∈ℕt\in{\mathbb{N}} and 𝒫:𝖥𝖲𝖦∙→{0,1}\mathcal{P}\colon\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\to\{0,1\}. Here we interpret 𝒫\mathcal{P} as a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm. Let 𝑮\bm{G} be a locally finite graph and suppose that we are given a function f:V⁡(𝑮)→ℕf\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}}. We say that ff is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G} if 𝒫​(𝑮f,t)​(x)=1\mathcal{P}(\bm{G}_{f},t)(x)=1 for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), i.e., if the output of the algorithm 𝒫\mathcal{P} on the structured graph 𝑮f\bm{G}_{f} after tt rounds is the constant 11 function.

What Definition 2.6 says is that, for a local coloring problem, there is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm, 𝒫\mathcal{P}, that, given a coloring ff, can verify whether ff is “correct” in a constant number of rounds, namely tt. To put this another way, whether or not a coloring ff is “correct” is completely determined by the restrictions of ff to balls of radius tt.

Example 2.7 (Proper coloring).

The prototypical example of a local coloring problem is proper kk-coloring of graphs, since whether or not a coloring is proper is determined by its restrictions to radius-11 balls. Explicitly, let k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} and define a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒫:𝖥𝖲𝖦∙→{0,1}\mathcal{P}\colon\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\to\{0,1\} as follows: Given (the isomorphism type of) a finite rooted structured graph of the form (G,f,x)(G,f,x) with f:V⁡(G)→[k]f\colon V(G)\to[k] and a root xx, set 𝒫⁡([G,f,x])≔1\mathcal{P}([G,f,x])\coloneqq 1 if and only if f⁡(y)≠f⁡(z)f(y)\neq f(z) for every pair of adjacent vertices yy, z∈V⁡(G)z\in V(G); in all other cases set 𝒫\mathcal{P} to 00. Now if we let Π≔(1,𝒫)\Pi\coloneqq(1,\mathcal{P}), then a Π\Pi-coloring of a locally finite graph GG is exactly the same as a proper kk-coloring of GG.

2.A.3.  Complexity of local coloring problems

As mentioned in the introduction, we must distinguish between the deterministic and the randomized versions of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model.

Definition 2.8 (Deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity).

Let Π\Pi be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Given n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, we write 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T if and only if there is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following property:

Let 𝑮\bm{G} be an nn-vertex structured graph such that [𝑮]∈𝖦[\bm{G}]\in\mathsf{G} and let 𝗂𝖽:V⁡(𝑮)→[n]\mathsf{id}\colon V(\bm{G})\to[n] be an arbitrary bijection. Then the function 𝒜⁡(𝑮𝗂𝖽,T)\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\mathsf{id}},T) is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}.

For n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}, define 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) to be the least T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}} such that 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T if such TT exists, and ∞\infty otherwise. The function 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦:ℕ+→ℕ∪{∞}\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}\colon{\mathbb{N}}^{+}\to{\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\infty\} is called the deterministic LOCAL\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of the problem Π\Pi on the class of structured graphs 𝖦\mathsf{G}.

Let us make a few remarks about the above definition. The set 𝖦\mathsf{G} in Definition 2.8 is the collection of (the isomorphism classes of) the finite structured graphs on which we attempt to solve the given coloring problem Π\Pi. For example, 𝖦\mathsf{G} may contain all graphs of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta, all triangle-free graphs, all trees, all cycles, all directed graphs, etc. If 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T, it means that there is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} that solves the problem Π\Pi on nn-vertex graphs 𝑮\bm{G} from the class 𝖦\mathsf{G} in TT rounds, given as part of its input an arbitrary assignment 𝗂𝖽\mathsf{id} of unique identifiers from the set [n][n] to the vertices of 𝑮\bm{G}. The reader may recall from the introduction that usually the identifiers are sequences of bits of length Θ⁡(log⁡n)\Theta(\log n), or, equivalently, elements of [nc][n^{c}] for some constant c⩾1c\geqslant 1. In practice it does not matter what constant cc one uses, so, for concreteness, we fix cc to be 11 (technically, making cc as small as possible only makes our main results stronger).

Definition 2.9 (Randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity).

Let Π\Pi be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Given n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, we write 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T if and only if there are m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} with the following property:

Let 𝑮\bm{G} be an nn-vertex structured graph such that [𝑮]∈𝖦[\bm{G}]\in\mathsf{G}. Pick a function ϑ:V⁡(𝑮)→[m]\vartheta\colon V(\bm{G})\to[m] uniformly at random (that is, each function V⁡(𝑮)→[m]V(\bm{G})\to[m] is chosen with probability 1/mn1/m^{n}). Then

ℙ⁡[𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T) is a Π-coloring of 𝑮]⩾ 1−1n.\mathbb{P}\left[\text{$\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T)$ is a $\Pi$-coloring of $\bm{G}$}\right]\,\geqslant\,1\,-\,\frac{1}{n}.

For n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}, define 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) to be the least T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}} such that 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T if such TT exists, and ∞\infty otherwise. The function 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦:ℕ+→ℕ∪{∞}\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}\colon{\mathbb{N}}^{+}\to{\mathbb{N}}\cup\{\infty\} is called the randomized LOCAL\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of the problem Π\Pi on the class of structured graphs 𝖦\mathsf{G}.

In Definition 2.9, 𝖦\mathsf{G} is again the class of finite structured graphs on which we wish to solve a given coloring problem. The algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} takes, as part of its input, an assignment of random numbers from [m][m] to the vertices of 𝑮\bm{G}, and, while it may fail to output a Π\Pi-coloring, the probability of failure cannot exceed 1/n1/n. Notice that there is no a priori upper bound on mm, i.e., the algorithm is allowed to use “unlimited randomness.” However, we do require that the same mm must work for all nn-vertex graphs 𝑮\bm{G} with [𝑮]∈𝖦[\bm{G}]\in\mathsf{G}. This restriction is harmless, at least for our purposes, as we shall only apply Definition 2.9 to classes 𝖦\mathsf{G} that contain finitely many isomorphism types of nn-vertex graphs for each nn.

2.B.  From distributed algorithms to descriptive combinatorics

2.B.1.  Deterministic algorithms and Borel colorings

We use standard descriptive set-theoretic terminology; see, e.g., Kechris’s book [Kec95] or Tserunyan’s notes [Tse16]. Recall that a separable topological space is Polish if its topology is induced by a complete metric. A standard Borel space is a set XX equipped with a σ\sigma-algebra 𝔅⁡(X)\mathfrak{B}(X) of Borel sets generated by a Polish topology on XX. We say that a Polish topology on a standard Borel space XX is compatible if it generates 𝔅⁡(X)\mathfrak{B}(X).

By a Borel graph we mean a graph GG whose vertex set V⁡(G)V(G) is a standard Borel space and such that {(x,y):x and y are adjacent in G}\{(x,y)\,:\,\text{$x$ and $y$ are adjacent in $G$}\} is a Borel subset of V⁡(G)×V⁡(G)V(G)\times V(G). Similarly, a Borel structured graph is a structured graph 𝑮=(G,σ)\bm{G}=(G,\sigma) such that GG is a Borel graph and σ:V​(G)<∞⇀ℕ\sigma\colon V(G)^{<\infty}\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} is a Borel function (which just means that for every c∈ℕc\in{\mathbb{N}}, σ−1​(c)\sigma^{-1}(c) is a Borel subset of V​(G)<∞V(G)^{<\infty}).

Let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG} be a collection of isomorphism types of finite structured graphs and let RR, n∈ℕn\in{\mathbb{N}}. We say that a structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in G\mathsf{G} if for each vertex x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), there is an nn-vertex structured graph 𝑯\bm{H} with [𝑯]∈𝖦[\bm{H}]\in\mathsf{G} such that [B𝑮​(x,R),x]=[B𝑯​(y,R),y][B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x]=[B_{\bm{H}}(y,R),y] for some y∈V⁡(𝑯)y\in V(\bm{H}). For instance, suppose that 𝖦\mathsf{G} is a class of finite graphs (with no other structure) closed under adding isolated vertices. Examples of such classes are the class of all planar graphs, the class of all graphs of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta for some fixed Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, the class of all triangle-free graphs, etc. It is not hard to see that in this case a graph GG is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} provided that for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), [BG​(x,R)]∈𝖦[B_{G}(x,R)]\in\mathsf{G} and |BG​(x,R)|⩽n|B_{G}(x,R)|\leqslant n. Now we can state our first result:

Theorem 2.10 (Deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms yield Borel colorings).

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)<∞\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)<\infty and set R≔𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)+tR\coloneqq\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)+t. If 𝑮\bm{G} is a Borel structured graph that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), then 𝑮\bm{G} has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring.

Note that a structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} satisfying the assumptions of Theorem 2.10 must have finite maximum degree, since |B𝑮​(x,R)|⩽n<∞|B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)|\leqslant n<\infty for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}).

Usually the precise value of 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) is not known and one only has access to asymptotic upper bounds. For instance, assume that 𝖦\mathsf{G} is a class of finite graphs (with no other structure), and let GG be a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta all of whose finite induced subgraphs are in 𝖦\mathsf{G}. We claim that if Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) is a local coloring problem such that 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)=o(\log n), then GG has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring. Indeed, we may assume that GG is infinite (otherwise GG itself is a finite graph in 𝖦\mathsf{G}, and hence it has an—automatically Borel—Π\Pi-coloring by assumption). This implies that 𝖦\mathsf{G} is closed under adding isolated vertices. Since tt is a constant independent of nn, R⁡(n)≔𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)+t=o⁡(log⁡n)R(n)\coloneqq\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)+t=o(\log n) as well. Therefore, for each x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G),

(2.11) |BG​(x,R⁡(n))|⩽|BG​(x,2​R​(n))|⩽ 1+Δ2​R​(n)= 1+Δo⁡(log⁡n)=no⁡(1).|B_{G}(x,R(n))|\,\leqslant\,|B_{G}(x,2R(n))|\,\leqslant\,1+\Delta^{2R(n)}\,=\,1+\Delta^{o(\log n)}\,=\,n^{o(1)}.

Thus, Theorem 2.10 may be applied for any large enough value of nn.

It is possible to incorporate into such calculations extra assumptions on the growth rate of GG. For example, say that a graph GG is of subexponential growth if for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is R0∈ℕR_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} such that if x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) and R⩾R0R\geqslant R_{0}, then |BG​(x,R)|<(1+ε)R|B_{G}(x,R)|<(1+\varepsilon)^{R}. As before, let 𝖦\mathsf{G} be a class of finite graphs and let GG be a Borel graph of subexponential growth all of whose finite induced subgraphs are in 𝖦\mathsf{G}. The same calculation as in the last paragraph shows that GG has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring whenever Π\Pi is a local coloring problem with 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)=O⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)=O(\log n). Stronger assumptions on the growth rate of GG enable one to further relax the necessary bound on 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n).

The reasoning in the preceding two paragraphs will apply, almost verbatim, to all the other results in this section.

2.B.2.  Deterministic algorithms and continuous colorings

Under certain circumstances, the word “Borel” in the conclusion of Theorem 2.10 can be replaced by “continuous.” In order to state this result precisely, we require a few definitions. In what follows, we view ℕ{\mathbb{N}} as a discrete topological space. Let (X,d)(X,d) be a metric space and let 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1}, 𝑮2\bm{G}_{2} be finite structured graphs with V⁡(𝑮1)V(\bm{G}_{1}), V⁡(𝑮2)⊆XV(\bm{G}_{2})\subseteq X. Given ε>0\varepsilon>0, we say that 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1} and 𝑮2\bm{G}_{2} are ε\varepsilon-isomorphic (with respect to the metric dd) if there is an isomorphism φ:V⁡(𝑮1)→V⁡(𝑮2)\varphi\colon V(\bm{G}_{1})\to V(\bm{G}_{2}) between 𝑮1\bm{G}_{1} and 𝑮2\bm{G}_{2} such that d⁡(x,φ⁡(x))<εd(x,\varphi(x))<\varepsilon for all x∈V⁡(𝑮1)x\in V(\bm{G}_{1}). Recall that a topological space is zero-dimensional is it has a base consisting of clopen sets.

Definition 2.12 (Topological graphs).

A topological structured graph is a locally finite structured graph 𝑮\bm{G} whose vertex set V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}) is a zero-dimensional Polish space and that has the following property for some (hence any) metric dd inducing the topology on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}): For each x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is δ>0\delta>0 such that if y∈V⁡(𝑮)y\in V(\bm{G}) satisfies d⁡(x,y)<δd(x,y)<\delta, then the rooted structured graphs (B𝑮​(x,R),x)(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x) and (B𝑮​(y,R),y)(B_{\bm{G}}(y,R),y) are ε\varepsilon-isomorphic.

Note that the above definition is indeed independent of the choice of the metric dd (we could have stated it purely topologically, by fixing an open neighborhood for each vertex in B𝑮​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R) instead of using the parameter ε\varepsilon). If we are hoping to find continuous colorings of 𝑮\bm{G}, it is natural to assume that the topology on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}) is zero-dimensional, so that V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}) has enough clopen subsets and hence there are many continuous functions V⁡(𝑮)→ℕV(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}}. The rest of Definition 2.12 describes the interplay between the combinatorics of 𝑮\bm{G} and the topology on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}). In particular, if 𝑮\bm{G} is a topological graph, then the map V⁡(𝑮)→𝖥𝖲𝖦∙:x↦[B𝑮​(x,R),x]V(\bm{G})\to\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\colon x\mapsto[B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x] is continuous for all R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, where we view the countable set 𝖥𝖲𝖦∙\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet} as a discrete space.

We prove a continuous version of Theorem 2.10 for topological graphs:

Theorem 2.13 (Deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms yield continuous colorings).

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)<∞\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)<\infty and set R≔𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)+tR\coloneqq\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)+t. If 𝑮\bm{G} is a topological structured graph that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), then 𝑮\bm{G} has a continuous Π\Pi-coloring.

Observe that Theorem 2.13 is a strengthening of Theorem 2.10. Indeed, it follows from standard results in descriptive set theory that if 𝑮\bm{G} is a locally finite Borel structured graph, then there is a compatible zero-dimensional Polish topology on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}) that makes 𝑮\bm{G} a topological structured graph [Kec95, §13]. (Nevertheless, we will give a direct proof of Theorem 2.10 as well.)

An ample supply of natural examples of topological graphs is provided by continuous actions of finitely generated groups. Let XX be a zero-dimensional Polish space and let Γ\Gamma be a group generated by a finite set S⊆ΓS\subseteq\Gamma. Assume additionally that SS does not contain the identity element of Γ\Gamma and that SS is symmetric, meaning that if γ∈S\gamma\in S, then γ−1∈S\gamma^{-1}\in S as well. Given a free action α:Γ↷X\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright X of Γ\Gamma on XX by homeomorphisms, let the Schreier graph of α\alpha be the graph GαG_{\alpha} with vertex set XX in which two vertices xx, y∈Xy\in X are adjacent if and only if x=γ⋅αyx=\gamma\cdot_{\alpha}y for some γ∈S\gamma\in S. Because α\alpha is free, it is easy to see that GαG_{\alpha} is a topological graph. If SS is not assumed to be symmetric, one can similarly define a directed version of the Schreier graph, which is a topological directed graph.

2.B.3.  Randomized algorithms

Recall that a set or a function is measurable (resp. Baire-measurable) if it differs from a Borel set or function on a null (resp. meager) set. In order to obtain measurable or Baire-measurable colorings, it is enough to work with randomized rather than deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms:

Theorem 2.14 (Randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms yield measurable colorings).

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)<∞\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)<\infty and set R≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)+tR\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)+t. Let 𝑮\bm{G} be a Borel structured graph that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n1/8/4|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n^{1/8}/4 for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}). Then the following conclusions hold:

  1. (i)

    If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}), then 𝑮\bm{G} has a μ\mu-measurable Π\Pi-coloring.

  2. (ii)

    If τ\tau is a compatible Polish topology on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}), then 𝑮\bm{G} has a τ\tau-Baire-measurable Π\Pi-coloring.

Although the bound on |B𝑮​(x,2​R)||B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)| required in Theorem 2.14 is stronger than that in Theorem 2.10, it remains polynomial in nn. In particular, inequalities (2.11) still show that if 𝖦\mathsf{G} is a class of finite graphs and GG is a Borel graph of finite maximum degree all of whose finite induced subgraphs are in 𝖦\mathsf{G}, then GG is measurably and Baire-measurably Π\Pi-colorable provided that 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)=o(\log n). Furthermore, if GG is of subexponential growth, then 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)=O⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)=O(\log n) suffices. Actually, in this case we can even make the coloring Borel:

Theorem 2.15 (Randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms yield Borel colorings of subexponential growth graphs).

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)<∞\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)<\infty and set R≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)+tR\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)+t. If 𝑮\bm{G} is a Borel structured graph of subexponential growth that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n/e|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n/e for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), then 𝑮\bm{G} has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring.

In the statement of Theorem 2.15, e=2.71​…e=2.71\ldots is the base of the natural logarithm. Theorem 2.15 contributes to the growing body of results showing that various combinatorial problems on graphs of subexponential growth can be solved in a Borel way, whereas in general one can only hope for a measurable solution; see, e.g., [Csó+22, CT21, Tho22].

2.C.  The Lovász Local Lemma

As mentioned in the introduction, the key ingredient in our proof of Theorem 2.14 is a new measurable version of the Lovász Local Lemma (the LLL for short), which is an interesting result in its own right. Indeed, the original motivation for this paper was to develop a better understanding of the behavior of the LLL in the measurable setting.

2.C.1.  Constraint satisfaction problems and the LLL

Recall that for a set AA, [A]<∞[A]^{<\infty} denotes the set of all finite subsets of AA. Similarly, for sets AA and BB, let [A⇀B]<∞[A\rightharpoonup B]^{<\infty} be the set of all partial functions φ:A⇀B\varphi\colon A\rightharpoonup B with finite domains.

Definition 2.16 (CSPs).

Fix a set XX and m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}. An (X,m)(X,m)-constraint (or simply a constraint if XX and mm are clear from the context) is a set B⊆[X⇀[m]]<∞B\subseteq[X\rightharpoonup[m]]^{<\infty} such that dom⁡(φ)=dom⁡(ψ)\mathrm{dom}(\varphi)=\mathrm{dom}(\psi) for all φ\varphi, ψ∈B\psi\in B. If a constraint BB is nonempty, then its domain is the set dom⁡(B)≔dom⁡(φ)\mathrm{dom}(B)\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(\varphi) for some (hence all) φ∈B\varphi\in B; the domain of the empty constraint is defined to be ∅\varnothing. A constraint satisfaction problem (a CSP for short) ℬ\mathscr{B} on XX with range [m][m], in symbols ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m], is a set of (X,m)(X,m)-constraints. A solution to a CSP ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] is a function f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m] such that for all B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}, the restriction f|dom⁡(B){{f}|{\mathrm{dom}(B)}} of ff onto dom⁡(B)\mathrm{dom}(B) is not a member of BB.

In other words, in a CSP ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m], each constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} is interpreted as a set of “forbidden patterns” that are not allowed to appear in a solution f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m]. There are obvious similarities between CSPs in the above sense and local colorings problems in the sense of Definition 2.6, and, indeed, a CSP can be viewed as local coloring problem on an auxiliary graph (see §5.D for details).

Fix a CSP ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m]. The probability ℙ⁡[B]\mathbb{P}[B] of a constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} is defined by

ℙ⁡[B]≔|B|m|dom⁡(B)|.\mathbb{P}[B]\,\coloneqq\,\frac{|B|}{m^{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|}}.

Notice that if we form a random coloring f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m] by assigning to each x∈Xx\in X a color from [m][m] uniformly at random, then ℙ⁡[B]\mathbb{P}[B] equals the probability that f|dom⁡(B)∈B{{f}|{\mathrm{dom}(B)}}\in B, i.e., that the constraint BB is violated by ff. The neighborhood of a constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} is the set N⁡(B)⊂ℬ\mathrm{N}(B)\subset\mathscr{B} given by

N⁡(B)≔{B′∈ℬ∖{B}:dom⁡(B′)∩dom⁡(B)≠∅}.\mathrm{N}(B)\,\coloneqq\,\{B^{\prime}\in\mathscr{B}\setminus\{B\}\,:\,\mathrm{dom}(B^{\prime})\cap\mathrm{dom}(B)\neq\varnothing\}.

The most widely used form of the LLL, called the Symmetric LLL, invokes the parameters

𝗉⁡(ℬ)≔supB∈ℬℙ⁡[B]and𝖽⁡(ℬ)≔supB∈ℬ|N⁡(B)|.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}\mathbb{P}[B]\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{B\in\mathscr{B}}|\mathrm{N}(B)|.
Theorem 2.17 (Symmetric LLL; see [AS00, Corollary 5.1.2]).

If ℬ\mathscr{B} is a CSP such that

(2.18) 𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)⩽e−1,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)\,\leqslant\,e^{-1},

where e=2.71​…e=2.71\ldots is the base of the natural logarithm, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution.

Theorem 2.17 is a special case of a stronger result, known as the General LLL, in which instead of bounding 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) uniformly, one establishes a more delicate—but somewhat less transparent—relationship between ℙ⁡[B]\mathbb{P}[B] and |N⁡(B)||\mathrm{N}(B)| for each constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}:

Theorem 2.19 (General LLL; see [AS00, Theorem 5.1.1]).

If ℬ\mathscr{B} is a CSP such that there is a function η:ℬ→[0,1)\eta\colon\mathscr{B}\to[0,1) satisfying

ℙ⁡[B]⩽η⁡(B)​∏B′∈N⁡(B)(1−η⁡(B′)),for all ​B∈ℬ,\mathbb{P}[B]\,\leqslant\,\eta(B)\prod_{B^{\prime}\in\mathrm{N}(B)}(1-\eta(B^{\prime})),\qquad\text{for all }B\in\mathscr{B},

then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution.

A standard calculation (see [AS00, proof of Corollary 5.1.2]) shows that the bound (2.18) implies the existence of a function η\eta as in Theorem 2.19, and hence the Symmetric LLL is indeed a special case of the General LLL. We remark that, due to its origin in finite combinatorics, the LLL is often stated in the case when the ground set XX is finite; however, the case of infinite XX follows via a straightforward compactness argument (see, e.g., [AS00, proof of Theorem 5.2.2]).

Several applications of the LLL in combinatorics and graph theory can be found in [AS00, MR02]. For most applications, the full power of the General LLL is not needed and the Symmetric LLL is sufficient. Furthermore, in many cases the bound (2.18) is quite far from being sharp: one can often prove that 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) is at most exp⁡(−log1+ε⁡𝖽⁡(ℬ))\exp(-\log^{1+\varepsilon}\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})) or even exp⁡(−𝖽​(ℬ)ε)\exp(-\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})^{\varepsilon}) for some constant ε>0\varepsilon>0. For example, this usually happens when the upper bound on 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) is obtained via a concentration of measure argument.

2.C.2.  Measurable Symmetric LLL

If XX is a standard Borel space, then [X]<∞[X]^{<\infty} also carries a natural standard Borel structure. Namely, a subset of [X]<∞[X]^{<\infty} is said to be Borel if and only if its preimage in ⨆k=0∞Xk\bigsqcup_{k=0}^{\infty}X^{k} under the map (x0,…,xk−1)↦{x0,…,xk−1}(x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1})\mapsto\{x_{0},\ldots,x_{k-1}\} is Borel. Next, for any standard Borel space YY, the set [X⇀Y]<∞[X\rightharpoonup Y]^{<\infty} also becomes a standard Borel space when viewed as a Borel subset of [X×Y]<∞[X\times Y]^{<\infty} by identifying each partial function φ∈[X⇀Y]<∞\varphi\in[X\rightharpoonup Y]^{<\infty} with its graph, i.e., with the set {(x,φ⁡(x)):x∈dom⁡(φ)}\{(x,\varphi(x))\,:\,x\in\mathrm{dom}(\varphi)\}. Finally, since, by definition, every (X,m)(X,m)-constraint is a finite set of partial functions with a common finite domain, the set of all (X,m)(X,m)-constraints is a Borel subset of [[X⇀[m]]<∞]<∞[[X\rightharpoonup[m]]^{<\infty}]^{<\infty}. Therefore, we may speak of Borel CSPs ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m], i.e., Borel sets of (X,m)(X,m)-constraints.

Given a Borel CSP, it is natural to ask whether it has a solution with some regularity properties. To that end, we establish the following measurable/Baire-measurable analog of Theorem 2.17 under a stronger polynomial bound on 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}):

Theorem 2.20 (Measurable Symmetric LLL).

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a Borel CSP such that

(2.21) 𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽ 2−15.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2^{-15}.

Assume additionally that sup{|dom⁡(B)|:B∈ℬ}<∞\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}<\infty. Then the following conclusions hold:

  1. (i)

    If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a μ\mu-measurable solution.

  2. (ii)

    If τ\tau is a compatible Polish topology on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a τ\tau-Baire-measurable solution.

As mentioned earlier, one can often bound 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) from above by a super-polynomially small function of 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}), making Theorem 2.20 applicable. We call CSPs ℬ\mathscr{B} such that sup{|dom⁡(B)|:B∈ℬ}<∞\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}<\infty bounded. The boundedness assumption in Theorem 2.20 can likely be eliminated by a routine modification of the proof. However, we are not aware of any applications where this assumption is not satisfied, and so we elected to include it in order to make our arguments more transparent.

Theorem 2.20 is implied by Theorem 2.14: a CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} can be encoded as a local coloring problem on an auxiliary graph (see §5.D for details), and Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] designed a randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that finds solutions to such local coloring problems in a sublogarithmic number of rounds under a polynomial bound on 𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}) and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}) similar to (2.21). The actual bound that we use comes from a sharpened version of the Fischer–Ghaffari algorithm developed in [GHK18] by Ghaffari, Harris, and Kuhn. Together with Theorem 2.14, their algorithm immediately yields Theorem 2.20. The logic of our argument, however, goes in the opposite direction: We shall first prove Theorem 2.20 and then derive Theorem 2.14 from it. Nevertheless, our proof of Theorem 2.20 does invoke the Ghaffari–Harris–Kuhn algorithm, albeit in a more subtle way.

2.C.3.  Comparison with prior work

The current state of the knowledge concerning the behavior of the LLL in the descriptive setting is summarized in Table 1. Conley, Jackson, Marks, Seward, and Tucker-Drob [Con+20, Theorem 1.6] constructed examples showing that the Symmetric LLL cannot, in general, produce Borel solutions. On the other hand, Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros [Csó+22] showed that a Borel version of the Symmetric LLL holds under certain subexponential growth assumptions on the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} (and we use their result to derive Theorem 2.15).

In the presence of a measure μ\mu, one can relax the requirements and only ask for a measurable function f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m] that satisfies the constraints on a set of measure 1−ε1-\varepsilon, for any given ε>0\varepsilon>0. In this regime, the Symmetric LLL always succeeds [Ber19, Theorem 5.1], while the General LLL may fail [Ber19, Theorem 7.1]. In fact, the General LLL may even fail to produce colorings that satisfy the constrains on a set of arbitrarily small positive measure. On the other hand, there are certain situations of particular interest in ergodic theory when the General LLL can be used to obtain measurable colorings satisfying all the constraints; namely, this happens when the structure of the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is, in a certain technical sense, “induced” by the Bernoulli shift action Γ↷[0,1]Γ\Gamma\curvearrowright[0,1]^{\Gamma} of a countable group Γ\Gamma [Ber19, Theorem 6.6].

Theorem 2.20 provides the first Baire-measurable variant of the LLL (with the exception of the subexponential Borel LLL of Csóka–Grabowski–Máthé–Pikhurko–Tyros). The following question remains open:

Open Problem 2.22.

Does there exist a Baire-measurable version of the General LLL?

3.  Applications

3.A.  Colorings with the number of colors close to Δ\Delta

Recall that the chromatic number χ⁡(G)\chi(G) of a graph GG is the smallest cardinality of a set YY such that GG admits a proper coloring f:V⁡(G)→Yf\colon V(G)\to Y. In the descriptive setting, one defines the Borel chromatic number χB​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G) of a Borel graph GG as the smallest cardinality of a standard Borel space YY such that GG has a Borel proper coloring f:V⁡(G)→Yf\colon V(G)\to Y. Similarly, given a probability Borel measure μ\mu or a compatible Polish topology τ\tau on V⁡(G)V(G), the μ\mu-measurable chromatic number χμ​(G)\chi_{\mu}(G) and the τ\tau-Baire-measurable chromatic number χτ​(G)\chi_{\tau}(G) are defined to be the smallest cardinality of a standard Borel space YY such that GG admits a μ\mu-measurable, resp. τ\tau-Baire-measurable, proper coloring f:V⁡(G)→Yf\colon V(G)\to Y. It is clear that χ⁡(G)⩽χμ​(G)\chi(G)\leqslant\chi_{\mu}(G), χτ​(G)⩽χB​(G)\chi_{\tau}(G)\leqslant\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G). We shall only work with bounded degree graphs, and for them all these parameters are finite:

Theorem 3.1 (Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic [KST99, Proposition 4.6]).

Let GG be a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta. Then χB​(G)⩽Δ+1\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant\Delta+1.

In general, the bound χ⁡(G)⩽Δ⁡(G)+1\chi(G)\leqslant\Delta(G)+1 is best possible, since a graph of maximum degree Δ\Delta may contain Δ+1\Delta+1 pairwise adjacent vertices (i.e., a (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-clique), all of which would have to receive distinct colors in a proper coloring of GG. Conversely, a classical theorem of Brooks (see [Die17, Theorem 5.2.4]) asserts that if χ⁡(G)=Δ⁡(G)+1\chi(G)=\Delta(G)+1 for a graph GG with 3⩽Δ⁡(G)<∞3\leqslant\Delta(G)<\infty, then GG contains a (Δ⁡(G)+1)(\Delta(G)+1)-clique.

It is natural to ask whether Brooks’s theorem can be extended to the setting of Borel, measurable, or Baire-measurable colorings. Marks [Mar16] showed that, in the Borel context, Brooks’s theorem fails in a very strong sense. A graph GG is called Δ\Delta-regular if every vertex in GG has degree Δ\Delta, and acyclic if it contains no cycles (acyclic graphs are also known as forests). It is easy to see that acyclic graphs are bipartite, i.e., have chromatic number at most 22. Nevertheless, Marks proved the following:

Theorem 3.2 (Marks [Mar16]).

For each Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, there exists an acyclic Δ\Delta-regular Borel graph GG such that χB​(G)=Δ+1\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)=\Delta+1.

In contrast to Theorem 3.2, Conley, Marks, and Tucker-Drob [CMT16] succeeded in extending Brooks’s theorem to the setting of measurable and Baire-measurable colorings:

Theorem 3.3 (Measurable Brooks; Conley–Marks–Tucker-Drob [CMT16]).

Let GG be a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3 without a (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-clique.

  1. (i)

    If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G), then χμ​(G)⩽Δ\chi_{\mu}(G)\leqslant\Delta.

  2. (ii)

    If τ\tau is a compatible Polish topology on V⁡(G)V(G), then χτ​(G)⩽Δ\chi_{\tau}(G)\leqslant\Delta.

In view of Brooks’s theorem, an equivalent way of phrasing Theorem 3.3 is that a Borel graph GG of finite maximum degree Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3 is measurably/Baire-measurably Δ\Delta-colorable if and only if it is Δ\Delta-colorable abstractly, i.e., without any regularity restrictions. Can this result be extended to colorings with fewer colors? We show that the answer is positive for (Δ−c)(\Delta-c)-colorings, where cc can be as large as roughly Δ\sqrt{\Delta}:

Theorem 3.4.

There is Δ0∈ℕ\Delta_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property. Fix integers Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0} and cc. Let GG be a Borel graph of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta and let μ\mu (resp. τ\tau) be a probability Borel measure (resp. a compatible Polish topology) on V⁡(G)V(G). If c⩽Δ+1/4−5/2c\leqslant\sqrt{\Delta+1/4}-5/2, then the following statements are equivalent:

  1. (i)

    χ⁡(G)⩽Δ−c\chi(G)\leqslant\Delta-c;

  2. (ii)

    χμ​(G)⩽Δ−c\chi_{\mu}(G)\leqslant\Delta-c;

  3. (iii)

    χτ​(G)⩽Δ−c\chi_{\tau}(G)\leqslant\Delta-c.

Proof.

Implications (ii), (iii) ⟹\Longrightarrow (i) are trivial, so we only need to argue that (i) ⟹\Longrightarrow (ii), (iii). For each k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, let Π⁡(k)\Pi(k) denote the local coloring problem that encodes proper kk-coloring of graphs (see Example 2.7). Fix Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} and c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} with c⩽Δ+1/4−5/2c\leqslant\sqrt{\Delta+1/4}-5/2 and let 𝖦⁡(Δ,c)\mathsf{G}(\Delta,c) be the set of all isomorphism classes of finite graphs GG of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta satisfying χ⁡(G)⩽Δ−c\chi(G)\leqslant\Delta-c. Assuming Δ\Delta is large enough, Bamas and Esperet [BE19, Theorem 1.3] established the following bounds on the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of proper (Δ−c)(\Delta-c)-coloring of graphs in 𝖦⁡(Δ,c)\mathsf{G}(\Delta,c):

(3.5) 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π⁡(Δ−c),𝖦⁡(Δ,c)​(n)⩽exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡log⁡n))=o⁡(log⁡n).\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi(\Delta-c),\mathsf{G}(\Delta,c)}(n)\,\leqslant\,\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n}))\,=\,o(\log n).

(Here the implicit constants in the asymptotic notation may depend on Δ\Delta, which we treat as fixed.) If GG is a Borel graph with Δ⁡(G)⩽Δ\Delta(G)\leqslant\Delta and χ⁡(G)⩽Δ−c\chi(G)\leqslant\Delta-c, then every finite induced subgraph of GG is in 𝖦⁡(Δ,c)\mathsf{G}(\Delta,c). Therefore, Theorem 2.14, combined with (3.5), yields that GG is both measurably and Baire-measurably (Δ−c)(\Delta-c)-colorable, as desired. ∎

Note that if in the statement of Theorem 3.4 we additionally assume that GG is of subexponential growth, then, replacing Theorem 2.14 by Theorem 2.15, we may conclude that for such GG, statements (i)–(iii) are also equivalent to

  1. (iv)

    χB​(G)⩽Δ−c\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant\Delta-c.

Marks’s Theorem 3.2 shows that the subexponential growth assumption cannot be removed.

The distributed algorithm of Bamas and Esperet [BE19] from which we derive Theorem 3.4 is inspired by the earlier work of Molloy and Reed [MR14] on sequential algorithms for (Δ−c)(\Delta-c)-coloring. Among other results, Molloy and Reed established the following remarkable extension of Brooks’s theorem: If Δ\Delta is large enough, GG is a graph of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta, and c⩽Δ+1/4−5/2c\leqslant\sqrt{\Delta+1/4}-5/2, then χ⁡(G)⩽Δ−c\chi(G)\leqslant\Delta-c if and only if χ⁡(BG​(x,1))⩽Δ−c\chi(B_{G}(x,1))\leqslant\Delta-c for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) [MR14, Theorem 5].

The bound on cc in the statement of Theorem 3.4 is almost sharp, in the sense that it cannot be relaxed to c⩽Δ−3/4−1/2c\leqslant\sqrt{\Delta-3/4}-1/2:

Proposition 3.6.

Let kk, Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} be such that Δ⩾k⩾2\Delta\geqslant k\geqslant 2 and Δ−k⩾Δ−3/4−1/2\Delta-k\geqslant\sqrt{\Delta-3/4}-1/2. Then there exist a Borel graph GG and a probability Borel measure μ\mu (resp. a compatible Polish topology τ\tau) on V⁡(G)V(G) such that Δ⁡(G)⩽Δ\Delta(G)\leqslant\Delta and χ⁡(G)⩽k\chi(G)\leqslant k but χμ​(G)>k\chi_{\mu}(G)>k (resp. χτ​(G)>k\chi_{\tau}(G)>k).

Proof.

We adapt the proof of [EHK98, Theorem 1.4] due to Embden-Weinert, Hougardy, and Kreuter. We shall give the argument for the measurable chromatic number, the Baire-measurable case being virtually identical. Fix k⩾2k\geqslant 2. To begin with, observe that there exists a Borel graph GG of finite maximum degree with a probability Borel measure μ\mu on V⁡(G)V(G) such that χ⁡(G)=k\chi(G)=k but χμ​(G)>k\chi_{\mu}(G)>k. For instance, let (X,μ)(X,\mu) be a standard probability space and let T:X→XT\colon X\to X be a measure-preserving transformation such that for all n∈ℤ∖{0}n\in\mathbb{Z}\setminus\{0\}, TnT^{n} is ergodic and Tn​(x)≠xT^{n}(x)\neq x for all x∈Xx\in X. An example of such a transformation is the map T:[0,1)→[0,1):x↦(x+α)​mod​ 1T\colon[0,1)\to[0,1)\colon x\mapsto(x+\alpha)\,\mathrm{mod}\,1, where α\alpha is a fixed irrational number. Let GG be the graph with vertex set XX in which two distinct vertices xx and yy are adjacent if and only if y=Tn​(x)y=T^{n}(x) with |n|⩽k−1|n|\leqslant k-1. It is easy to verify that χ⁡(G)=k\chi(G)=k and every proper kk-coloring f:X→[k]f\colon X\to[k] of GG is TkT^{k}-periodic, meaning that f⁡(Tk​(x))=f⁡(x)f(T^{k}(x))=f(x) for all x∈Xx\in X. To show that χμ​(G)>k\chi_{\mu}(G)>k, suppose that f:X→[k]f\colon X\to[k] is a measurable proper kk-coloring. Then every color class of ff is a TkT^{k}-invariant measurable subset of XX. Since the map TkT^{k} is ergodic, this implies that precisely one color class of ff is conull, while the other k−1k-1 classes are null. This is a contradiction, as the map TT cyclically permutes the color classes, showing that they all must have the same measure.

Now let Δ⩾k\Delta\geqslant k satisfy Δ−k⩾Δ−3/4−1/2\Delta-k\geqslant\sqrt{\Delta-3/4}-1/2 and let GG be a Borel graph with a probability Borel measure μ\mu on V⁡(G)V(G) such that χ⁡(G)⩽k\chi(G)\leqslant k, χμ​(G)>k\chi_{\mu}(G)>k, and Δ⁡(G)\Delta(G) is the smallest among all graphs with these properties. Set d≔Δ⁡(G)d\coloneqq\Delta(G) and c≔d−kc\coloneqq d-k. Suppose, toward a contradiction, that d>Δd>\Delta. Then c>d−3/4−1/2c>\sqrt{d-3/4}-1/2, which implies that c⁡(c+1)>d−1c(c+1)>d-1. Since cc and dd are integers, this yields c⁡(c+1)⩾dc(c+1)\geqslant d. Fix a Borel linear order << on V⁡(G)V(G) (such an order exists since, by [Kec95, Theorem 15.6], V⁡(G)V(G) is isomorphic to a Borel subset of ℝ\mathbb{R}). For each x∈Xx\in X and 1⩽i⩽degG⁡(x)1\leqslant i\leqslant\deg_{G}(x), let Ni​(x)N_{i}(x) be the ii-th neighbor of xx in the order <<; that is, we have

NG​(x)={N1​(x),…,NdegG⁡(x)​(x)}andN1​(x)<⋯<NdegG⁡(x)​(x).N_{G}(x)\,=\,\{N_{1}(x),\ldots,N_{\deg_{G}(x)}(x)\}\qquad\text{and}\qquad N_{1}(x)\,<\,\cdots\,<\,N_{\deg_{G}(x)}(x).

For α∈ℤ/(c+1)​ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}/(c+1)\mathbb{Z}, let Nα​(x)≔{Ni​(x):α=i​mod​(c+1)}N_{\alpha}(x)\coloneqq\{N_{i}(x)\,:\,\alpha=i\,\mathrm{mod}\,(c+1)\}. Note that |Nα​(x)|⩽⌈degG⁡(x)/(c+1)⌉⩽c|N_{\alpha}(x)|\leqslant\lceil\deg_{G}(x)/(c+1)\rceil\leqslant c, where we are using that c⁡(c+1)⩾dc(c+1)\geqslant d. Define a graph HH as follows. The vertex set of HH is

V⁡(H)≔V⁡(G)×((ℤ/(c+1)​ℤ)⊔[k−1]).V(H)\,\coloneqq\,V(G)\times((\mathbb{Z}/(c+1)\mathbb{Z})\sqcup[k-1]).

For clarity, let uα​(x)≔(x,α)u_{\alpha}(x)\coloneqq(x,\alpha) and vi​(x)≔(x,i)v_{i}(x)\coloneqq(x,i) for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), α∈ℤ/(c+1)​ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}/(c+1)\mathbb{Z}, and i∈[k−1]i\in[k-1]. Make the following pairs of vertices adjacent in HH:

  • —

    vi​(x)v_{i}(x) and vj​(x)v_{j}(x) for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) and distinct ii, j∈[k−1]j\in[k-1];

  • —

    vi​(x)v_{i}(x) and uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), i∈[k−1]i\in[k-1], and α∈ℤ/(c+1)​ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}/(c+1)\mathbb{Z};

  • —

    uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) and uβ​(y)u_{\beta}(y) for all adjacent xx, y∈V⁡(G)y\in V(G) with y∈Nα​(x)y\in N_{\alpha}(x) and x∈Nβ​(y)x\in N_{\beta}(y).

Let ν\nu be the pushforward of μ\mu under the map V⁡(G)→V⁡(H):x↦u0​(x)V(G)\to V(H)\colon x\mapsto u_{0}(x). We will show that HH satisfies χ⁡(H)⩽k\chi(H)\leqslant k, χν​(H)>k\chi_{\nu}(H)>k, and Δ⁡(H)⩽d−1\Delta(H)\leqslant d-1, which contradicts the choice of GG and thus completes the proof of Proposition 3.6.

To see that HH is kk-colorable, let f:V⁡(G)→[k]f\colon V(G)\to[k] be any kk-coloring of GG and define h:V⁡(H)→[k]h\colon V(H)\to[k] as follows: For all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) and α∈ℤ/(c+1)​ℤ\alpha\in\mathbb{Z}/(c+1)\mathbb{Z}, set h⁡(uα​(x))≔f⁡(x)h(u_{\alpha}(x))\coloneqq f(x), and assign to the vertices v1​(x)v_{1}(x), …, vk−1​(x)v_{k-1}(x) the k−1k-1 colors distinct from f⁡(x)f(x). Then hh is a proper kk-coloring of HH, so χ⁡(H)⩽k\chi(H)\leqslant k. To show that χν​(H)>k\chi_{\nu}(H)>k, suppose that h:V⁡(H)→[k]h\colon V(H)\to[k] is a ν\nu-measurable kk-coloring of HH. By the definition of ν\nu, the map f:V⁡(G)→[k]:x↦h⁡(u0​(x))f\colon V(G)\to[k]\colon x\mapsto h(u_{0}(x)) is μ\mu-measurable, and we claim that it is a proper kk-coloring of GG, which is impossible. Consider any two adjacent vertices xx, y∈V⁡(G)y\in V(G). Since the vertices v1​(x)v_{1}(x), …, vk−1​(x)v_{k-1}(x) are pairwise adjacent in HH, there is precisely one color that is not used by hh on any of them, and that must be the color assigned to every vertex of the form uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x). Similarly, all the vertices of the form uβ​(y)u_{\beta}(y) have the same color. Let α\alpha, β∈ℤ/(c+1)​ℤ\beta\in\mathbb{Z}/(c+1)\mathbb{Z} be such that y∈Nα​(x)y\in N_{\alpha}(x) and x∈Nβ​(y)x\in N_{\beta}(y). Then the vertices uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) and uβ​(y)u_{\beta}(y) are adjacent, so f⁡(x)=h⁡(u0​(x))=h⁡(uα​(x))≠h⁡(uβ​(y))=h⁡(u0​(y))=f⁡(y)f(x)=h(u_{0}(x))=h(u_{\alpha}(x))\neq h(u_{\beta}(y))=h(u_{0}(y))=f(y), as desired. It remains to verify that Δ⁡(H)⩽d−1\Delta(H)\leqslant d-1. To this end, note that every vertex of the form vi​(x)v_{i}(x) has degree

degH⁡(vi​(x))=(k−2)+(c+1)=d−1,\deg_{H}(v_{i}(x))\,=\,(k-2)\,+\,(c+1)\,=\,d-1,

while every vertex of the form uα​(x)u_{\alpha}(x) has degree

degH⁡(uα​(x))=(k−1)+|Nα​(x)|⩽k−1+c=d−1.∎\deg_{H}(u_{\alpha}(x))\,=\,(k-1)\,+\,|N_{\alpha}(x)|\,\leqslant\,k-1+c\,=\,d-1.\qed

There is a small gap between the bounds in Theorem 3.4 and Proposition 3.6. We leave closing this gap as an open problem:

Open Problem 3.7.

For each Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}}, determine precisely the largest value of c∈ℤc\in\mathbb{Z} for which the conclusion of Theorem 3.4 holds.

Theorem 3.4 implies Theorem 3.3, i.e., the measurable version of Brooks’s theorem, for all large enough Δ\Delta. One can actually use distributed algorithms to deduce Theorem 3.3 for all Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3. Indeed, Ghaffari, Hirvonen, Kuhn, and Maus [Gha+18] developed a randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm that, given an nn-vertex graph GG of maximum degree Δ⩾3\Delta\geqslant 3 and without a complete subgraph on Δ+1\Delta+1 vertices, finds a proper Δ\Delta-coloring of GG in O⁡((log⁡log⁡n)2)=o⁡(log⁡n)O((\log\log n)^{2})=o(\log n) rounds (here, as in (3.5), the implicit constants in the asymptotic notation may depend on Δ\Delta). Combined with Theorem 2.14, this yields Theorem 3.3.

3.B.  Graphs without short cycles

The distinctions between the three regularity notions—“Borel,” “measurable,” and “Baire-measurable”—are clearly demonstrated by colorings of acyclic graphs. Recall that, by Marks’s Theorem 3.2, the Borel chromatic number of an acyclic Borel graph of maximum degree Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} can be as large as Δ+1\Delta+1. In contrast to this, the Baire-measurable chromatic number of a locally finite acyclic graph is always at most 33, which is a consequence of the following general result of Conley and Miller:

Theorem 3.8 (Conley–Miller [CM16]).

Let GG be a locally finite Borel graph and let τ\tau be a compatible Polish topology on V⁡(G)V(G). If χ⁡(G)\chi(G) is finite, then χτ​(G)⩽2​χ​(G)−1\chi_{\tau}(G)\leqslant 2\chi(G)-1.

Since χ⁡(G)⩽2\chi(G)\leqslant 2 for an acyclic graph GG, Theorem 3.8 implies that the Baire-measurable chromatic number of an acyclic locally finite Borel graph is indeed at most 2⋅2−1=32\cdot 2-1=3. It is also not hard to see that this upper bound is best possible; see, e.g., [CMT16, §6].

Now we turn to measurable colorings. Lyons and Nazarov [LN11] (see also [KM19, Theorem 5.46]) constructed acyclic Borel graphs with maximum degree Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} and measurable chromatic number at least (1/2+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ(1/2+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta. This shows that acyclic Borel graphs of bounded degree can have arbitrarily large measurable chromatic numbers, contrary to the situation with Baire-measurable colorings. Although the present author showed [Ber19, Corollary 1.2] that Θ⁡(Δ/log⁡Δ)\Theta(\Delta/\log\Delta) is the correct order of magnitude in the Lyons–Nazarov examples, the best heretofore known general upper bound on measurable chromatic numbers of acyclic graphs in terms of their maximum degree was Δ\Delta, which is a consequence of the measurable Brooks’s Theorem 3.3 of Conley–Marks–Tucker-Drob. Here we improve this to (1+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ(1+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta, which falls within a factor of 22 of best possible. Furthermore, we do not even require acyclicity—it suffices to only forbid cycles of length at most 44.

Theorem 3.9.

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is Δ0∈ℕ\Delta_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property. Let GG be a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0} and let μ\mu be a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G).

  1. (i)

    If GG contains no cycles of length at most 44, then χμ​(G)⩽(1+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ\chi_{\mu}(G)\leqslant(1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta.

  2. (ii)

    If GG contains no cycles of length 33, then χμ​(G)⩽(4+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ\chi_{\mu}(G)\leqslant(4+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta.

Proof.

To derive this theorem, we invoke the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms for graph coloring developed by Chung, Pettie, and Su in [CPS17]. We shall first prove (ii). For each k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}}, let Π⁡(k)\Pi(k) denote the local coloring problem that encodes proper kk-coloring of graphs (see Example 2.7). Fix ε>0\varepsilon>0 and Δ∈ℕ\Delta\in{\mathbb{N}} and set k≔⌊(4+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ⌋k\coloneqq\lfloor(4+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta\rfloor. Let 𝖦⁡(Δ)\mathsf{G}(\Delta) be the set of all isomorphism classes of finite graphs of maximum degree at most Δ\Delta with no 33-cycles. It follows from [CPS17, Theorem 9] that there exist positive real numbers CC and δ\delta, depending only on ε\varepsilon, such that, for all large enough Δ\Delta and nn,

(3.10) 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π⁡(k),𝖦⁡(Δ)​(n)⩽C​Δ−δ​log⁡n.\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi(k),\mathsf{G}(\Delta)}(n)\,\leqslant\,C\Delta^{-\delta}\log n.

Even though this upper bound is weaker than o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n), it still suffices for an application of Theorem 2.14. Indeed, let GG be a Borel graph of maximum degree Δ\Delta without cycles of length 33 and set R⁡(n)≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π⁡(k),𝖦⁡(Δ)​(n)+1R(n)\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi(k),\mathsf{G}(\Delta)}(n)+1. If Δ\Delta is large enough and nn is much larger than Δ\Delta, then for each vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G),

|BG​(x,2​R​(n))|⩽ 1+Δ2​C​Δ−δ​log⁡n+2= 1+exp⁡(2​C​Δ−δ​log​Δ​log​n+2​log​Δ)<n1/8/4.|B_{G}(x,2R(n))|\,\leqslant\,1+\Delta^{2C\Delta^{-\delta}\log n+2}\,=\,1+\exp(2C\Delta^{-\delta}\log\Delta\log n+2\log\Delta)\,<\,n^{1/8}/4.

Similarly, |BG​(x,R⁡(n))|<n|B_{G}(x,R(n))|<n, and, since 𝖦⁡(Δ)\mathsf{G}(\Delta) is closed under adding isolated vertices, GG is (R⁡(n),n)(R(n),n)-locally in 𝖦⁡(Δ)\mathsf{G}(\Delta). Hence, Theorem 2.14 allows us to conclude that GG is measurably kk-colorable, which proves (ii). The proof of (i) is virtually the same, except that [CPS17, Theorem 9] is replaced by the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm of Chung, Pettie, and Su for ((1+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ)((1+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta)-coloring graphs without cycles of length at most 44 (see the remark in [CPS17] after [CPS17, Theorem 9]). ∎

Again, if GG is of subexponential growth, then, due to Theorem 2.15, the upper bounds on χμ​(G)\chi_{\mu}(G) given by Theorem 3.9 also hold for χB​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G).

We remark that, although this was not needed in the proof of Theorem 3.9, the bound (3.10) can actually be improved to 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π⁡(k),𝖦⁡(Δ)​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi(k),\mathsf{G}(\Delta)}(n)=o(\log n). Indeed, the algorithm developed by Chung, Pettie, and Su in order to prove (3.10) invokes as a subroutine a certain distributed version of the LLL. Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] later designed a more efficient distributed version of the LLL, and using their result reduces the complexity of the Chung–Pettie–Su algorithm to o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n).

The upper bound χ⁡(G)⩽(1+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ\chi(G)\leqslant(1+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta for finite graphs GG without cycles of length at most 44 is due to Kim [Kim95]. The existence of a constant C>0C>0 such that χ⁡(G)⩽(C+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ\chi(G)\leqslant(C+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta for finite graphs GG without 33-cycles was first established by Johansson [Joh96] (Johansson’s original paper is hard to access, but a detailed presentation of his argument can be found in [MR02, §13]). Johansson’s original proof gave the value C=9C=9. Pettie and Su [PS15] improved this to C=4C=4 (which is the value appearing in Theorem 3.9). Recently, Molloy [Mol19] further reduced the constant to C=1C=1. We leave the question of whether Molloy’s result also holds for measurable colorings as an open problem:

Open Problem 3.11.

Is it true that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is Δ0∈ℕ\Delta_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property? Let GG be a Borel graph of finite maximum degree Δ⩾Δ0\Delta\geqslant\Delta_{0} and let μ\mu be a probability Borel measure on V⁡(G)V(G). If GG contains no cycles of length 33, then χμ​(G)⩽(1+ε)​Δ/log⁡Δ\chi_{\mu}(G)\leqslant(1+\varepsilon)\Delta/\log\Delta.

One way to solve Problem 3.11 would be to develop a sublogarithmic randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for ((1+o⁡(1))​Δ/log⁡Δ)((1+o(1))\Delta/\log\Delta)-coloring graphs without 33-cycles.

3.C.  A result on list-coloring

In this section we apply Theorem 2.14 to obtain a useful result concerning list-colorings of Borel graphs. For an introduction to the theory of list-coloring, see [Die17, §5.4]. A list assignment for a graph GG is a function L:V⁡(G)→[ℕ]<∞L\colon V(G)\to[{\mathbb{N}}]^{<\infty}. For each vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), the set L⁡(x)L(x) is called the list of xx, and the elements of L⁡(x)L(x) are the colors available to xx. An LL-coloring of GG is a map f:V⁡(G)→ℕf\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} such that f⁡(x)∈L⁡(x)f(x)\in L(x) for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G). An LL-coloring ff is proper if f⁡(x)≠f⁡(y)f(x)\neq f(y) whenever xx and yy are adjacent in GG. We say that LL is an (ℓ,d)(\ell,d)-list assignment if it has the following two properties:

  • —

    for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), |L⁡(x)|⩾ℓ|L(x)|\geqslant\ell; and

  • —

    for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) and α∈L⁡(x)\alpha\in L(x), |{y∈NG​(x):α∈L⁡(y)}|⩽d|\{y\in N_{G}(x)\,:\,\alpha\in L(y)\}|\leqslant d.

The following is a result of Reed and Sudakov:

Theorem 3.12 (Reed–Sudakov [RS02]).

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is d0∈ℕd_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property. Let GG be a graph and let LL be an (ℓ,d)(\ell,d)-list assignment for GG, where d⩾d0d\geqslant d_{0} and ℓ⩾(1+ε)​d\ell\geqslant(1+\varepsilon)d. Then GG admits a proper LL-coloring.

A version of Theorem 3.12 with the bound ℓ⩾(1+ε)​d\ell\geqslant(1+\varepsilon)d replaced by ℓ⩾2​e​d\ell\geqslant 2ed was first proved by Reed [Ree99]; this was then improved by Haxell [Hax01] to ℓ⩾2​d\ell\geqslant 2d. While it is weaker than Theorem 3.12 for large dd, Haxell’s result holds for all positive integers dd and not only for sufficiently large ones. Reed [Ree99] conjectured that in fact ℓ⩾d+1\ell\geqslant d+1 should suffice, but this conjecture was refuted by Bohman and Holzman [BH02].

Theorem 3.12 (or its weaker versions mentioned in the previous paragraph) is a somewhat technical but rather useful fact that plays a crucial role in the proofs of many graph coloring results (see [MR02] for a number of examples). Here we establish a version of Theorem 3.12 for measurable and Baire-measurable colorings:

Theorem 3.13.

For every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is d0∈ℕd_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} with the following property. Let GG be a Borel graph and let LL be a Borel (ℓ,d)(\ell,d)-list assignment for GG, where d⩾d0d\geqslant d_{0} and ℓ⩾(1+ε)​d\ell\geqslant(1+\varepsilon)d. Let μ\mu (resp. τ\tau) be a probability Borel measure (resp. a compatible Polish topology) on V⁡(G)V(G). Then GG admits a μ\mu-measurable (resp. τ\tau-Baire-measurable) proper LL-coloring.

Proof.

We shall use another 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm due to Chung, Pettie, and Su [CPS17]. As explained in Example 2.4, we can interpret pairs (G,L)(G,L), where GG is a graph and LL a list assignment for GG, as structured graphs in the sense of Definition 2.1. Furthermore, proper list-coloring can naturally be encoded as a local coloring problem Π\Pi. Explicitly, let 𝒫:𝖥𝖲𝖦∙→{0,1}\mathcal{P}\colon\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\to\{0,1\} be the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm defined as follows: Given (the isomorphism type of) a finite rooted structured graph of the form (G,L,f,x)(G,L,f,x) with LL a list assignment for GG and f:V⁡(G)→ℕf\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}}, set 𝒫⁡([G,L,f,x])≔1\mathcal{P}([G,L,f,x])\coloneqq 1 if and only if ff is a proper LL-coloring of GG; in all other cases set 𝒫\mathcal{P} to 00.
