Now if we let Π≔(1,𝒫)\Pi\coloneqq(1,\mathcal{P}), then a Π\Pi-coloring of (G,L)(G,L) is precisely the same as a proper LL-coloring of GG.

Let 𝖦⁡(ℓ,d)⊂𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}(\ell,d)\subset\mathsf{FSG} denote the set of all isomorphism types of finite structured graphs corresponding to pairs of the form (G,L)(G,L), where GG is a finite graph and LL is an (ℓ,d)(\ell,d)-list assignment for GG. The result of Chung, Pettie, and Su presented in [CPS17, §4.4] implies that for every ε>0\varepsilon>0, there exist positive real numbers CC and δ\delta such that, for all large enough dd and nn,

(3.14) 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦⁡((1+ε)​d,d)​(n)⩽C​d−δ​log⁡n.\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}((1+\varepsilon)d,d)}(n)\,\leqslant\,Cd^{-\delta}\log n.

As in the proof of Theorem 3.9, this upper bound is weaker than o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) but sufficient for an application of Theorem 2.14. Indeed, let GG be a Borel graph and let LL be a Borel ((1+ε)​d,d)((1+\varepsilon)d,d)-list assignment for GG, where dd is a large positive integer. Without loss of generality, we may assume that |L⁡(x)|=ℓ|L(x)|=\ell for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G), and, by removing from GG all the edges x​yxy such that L⁡(x)∩L⁡(y)=∅L(x)\cap L(y)=\varnothing, we may arrange that Δ⁡(G)⩽(1+ε)​d2⩽d3\Delta(G)\leqslant(1+\varepsilon)d^{2}\leqslant d^{3}. Set R⁡(n)≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦⁡((1+ε)​d,d)​(n)+1R(n)\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}((1+\varepsilon)d,d)}(n)+1. For all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G),

|BG​(x,2​R​(n))|⩽ 1+d6​C​d−δ​log⁡n+6= 1+exp⁡(6​C​d−δ​log​d​log​n+6​log​d)<n1/8/4,|B_{G}(x,2R(n))|\,\leqslant\,1+d^{6Cd^{-\delta}\log n+6}\,=\,1+\exp(6Cd^{-\delta}\log d\log n+6\log d)\,<\,n^{1/8}/4,

where the last inequality holds whenever dd and nn are large enough. Similarly, |BG​(x,R⁡(n))|<n|B_{G}(x,R(n))|<n, and hence the pair (G,L)(G,L) is (R⁡(n),n)(R(n),n)-locally in 𝖦⁡((1+ε)​d,d)\mathsf{G}((1+\varepsilon)d,d). Therefore, by Theorem 2.14, GG admits a measurable/Baire-measurable proper LL-coloring, as desired. ∎

Again, for graphs of subexponential growth, we can use Theorem 2.15 to upgrade the conclusion of Theorem 3.13 to a Borel proper LL-coloring. Like (3.10), the bound (3.14) can be improved to 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦⁡((1+ε)​d,d)​(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}((1+\varepsilon)d,d)}(n)=o(\log n) by using the Fischer–Ghaffari distributed LLL [FG17].

3.D.  Sparse graphs

Among the oldest topics in graph theory is studying colorings of planar graphs. For the purposes of this paper, we say that an infinite graph is planar if all its finite subgraphs are planar. One of the most celebrated results in graph theory is the Four Color Theorem of Appel and Haken [Die17, Theorem 5.1.1] that asserts that χ⁡(G)⩽4\chi(G)\leqslant 4 for all planar graphs GG. Furthermore, if GG is a planar graph without 33-cycles, then χ⁡(G)⩽3\chi(G)\leqslant 3—this is a theorem of Grötzsch [Die17, Theorem 5.1.3]. On the other hand, the Lyons–Nazarov examples [LN11] mentioned in §3.B (see also [KM19, Theorem 5.46]) show that bounded degree acyclic (hence planar) Borel graphs can have arbitrarily large measurable chromatic numbers. Nevertheless, we show that under the additional assumption of subexponential growth, Borel chromatic numbers of planar Borel graphs are bounded by 55, and can be further lowered for graphs without short cycles:

Theorem 3.15.

Let GG be a planar Borel graph of subexponential growth and define

k≔{3if G contains no cycles of length at most 4;4if G contains a 4-cycle but no 3-cycles;5otherwise.k\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}3&\text{if $G$ contains no cycles of length at most $4$};\\ 4&\text{if $G$ contains a $4$-cycle but no $3$-cycles};\\ 5&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Then χB​(G)⩽k\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant k. Furthermore, if GG is also a topological graph (in the sense of Definition 2.12), then GG admits a continuous proper kk-coloring.

Proof.

This is a consequence of the recent work of Postle [Pos19]. Let 𝖯\mathsf{P} denote the set of all isomorphism classes of finite planar graphs and let 𝖯⁡(g)⊆𝖯\mathsf{P}(g)\subseteq\mathsf{P} be the set of all isomorphism classes of finite planar graphs without cycles of length strictly less than gg. Letting Π⁡(k)\Pi(k) denote the local coloring problem corresponding to proper kk-coloring (see Example 2.7), Postle [Pos19, Theorem 1.3] established the following bounds:

max⁡{𝖣𝖾𝗍Π⁡(5),𝖯​(n),𝖣𝖾𝗍Π⁡(4),𝖯⁡(4)​(n),𝖣𝖾𝗍Π⁡(3),𝖯⁡(5)​(n)}=O⁡(log⁡n).\max\{\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi(5),\mathsf{P}}(n),\,\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi(4),\mathsf{P}(4)}(n),\,\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi(3),\mathsf{P}(5)}(n)\}\,=\,O(\log n).

Combined with Theorems 2.10 and 2.13, this yields the desired results. (Theorems 2.10 and 2.13 may be applied as graphs of subexponential growth have finite maximum degree.) ∎

An important feature of planar graphs is their sparsity: by Euler’s formula, a planar graph GG with n⩾3n\geqslant 3 vertices can have at most 3​n−63n-6 edges. A convenient measure of sparsity for an arbitrary graph is its arboricity, defined as follows. Recall that |G||G| and ‖G‖\|G\| are the cardinalities of the vertex and the edge sets of GG, respectively. The arboricity of a graph GG with |G|⩾2|G|\geqslant 2 is the quantity

a⁡(G)≔supH⌈‖H‖|H|−1⌉,a(G)\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{H}\left\lceil\frac{\|H\|}{|H|-1}\right\rceil,

where the supremum is taken over all the finite subgraphs HH of GG with |H|⩾2|H|\geqslant 2. For graphs GG with |G|⩽1|G|\leqslant 1, a⁡(G)≔0a(G)\coloneqq 0 by definition. A theorem of Nash-Williams [Die17, Theorem 2.4.4] asserts that if GG is a finite graph, then a⁡(G)a(G) is equal to the smallest k∈ℕk\in{\mathbb{N}} such that GG has kk acyclic subgraphs F1F_{1}, …, FkF_{k} with E⁡(G)=E⁡(F1)∪…∪E⁡(Fk)E(G)=E(F_{1})\cup\ldots\cup E(F_{k}). Since acyclic graphs are also called “forests,” this explains the term “arboricity.”

Many classes of graphs have bounded arboricity. For instance, all planar graphs have arboricity at most 33. It is not hard to see that graphs GG of finite arboricity satisfy χ⁡(G)⩽2​a​(G)\chi(G)\leqslant 2a(G) (and this bound is, in general, best possible). On the other hand, the measurable chromatic number of a bounded degree acyclic (i.e., arboricity 11) Borel graph can be arbitrarily large. As in the case of planar graphs, the situation improves under the subexponential growth assumption:

Theorem 3.16.

If GG is a Borel graph of subexponential growth, then χB​(G)⩽2​a​(G)+1\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant 2a(G)+1. Furthermore, if GG is also a topological graph, then GG admits a continuous proper (2​a​(G)+1)(2a(G)+1)-coloring.

Proof.

Let 𝖦⁡(a)\mathsf{G}(a) denote the set of all isomorphism classes of finite graphs of arboricity at most aa, and let Π⁡(k)\Pi(k) be the local coloring problem corresponding to proper kk-coloring. Barenboim and Elkin [BE10, §4] proved that for all a∈ℕa\in{\mathbb{N}},

𝖣𝖾𝗍Π⁡(2​a+1),𝖦⁡(a)=O⁡(log⁡n),\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi(2a+1),\mathsf{G}(a)}\,=\,O(\log n),

where the implicit constants in the asymptotic notation may depend on aa. (The statement in [BE10, §4] is more general and involves an additional positive parameter ε\varepsilon; the bound that we need is obtained by setting ε=1/(a+1)\varepsilon=1/(a+1).) It remains to apply Theorems 2.10 and 2.13. ∎

The bound χB​(G)⩽2​a​(G)+1\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant 2a(G)+1 for Borel graphs GG of subexponential growth is, in general, sharp, since there exist acyclic 22-regular Borel graphs GG with χB​(G)=3\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)=3, and such graphs are of subexponential (in fact, linear) growth; see, e.g., [CMT16, §6]. Nevertheless, we conjecture that acyclic graphs are an exception and the bound χB​(G)⩽2​a​(G)\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant 2a(G) should hold whenever a⁡(G)⩾2a(G)\geqslant 2:

Conjecture 3.17.

If GG is a Borel graph of subexponential growth, then χB​(G)⩽max⁡{2​a​(G),3}\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant\max\{2a(G),3\}.

As evidence for Conjecture 3.17, we show that it holds for graphs whose order of growth is somewhat lower than just subexponential:

Theorem 3.18.

Let GG be a Borel graph and suppose that for each ε>0\varepsilon>0, there is R0∈ℕR_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}} such that if x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) and R⩾R0R\geqslant R_{0}, then |BG​(x,R)|<exp⁡(ε​R1/3)|B_{G}(x,R)|<\exp(\varepsilon R^{1/3}). Then χB​(G)⩽max⁡{2​a​(G),3}\chi_{\mathrm{B}}(G)\leqslant\max\{2a(G),3\}. Furthermore, if GG is also a topological graph, then GG admits a continuous proper max⁡{2​a​(G),3}\max\{2a(G),3\}-coloring.

Proof.

As in the proof of Theorem 3.16, let 𝖦⁡(a)\mathsf{G}(a) be the set of all isomorphism classes of finite graphs of arboricity at most aa, and let Π⁡(k)\Pi(k) be the local coloring problem encoding proper kk-coloring. Aboulker, Bonamy, Bousquet, and Esperet [Abo+19, Corollary 1.4] showed that for a⩾2a\geqslant 2,

𝖣𝖾𝗍Π⁡(2​a),𝖦⁡(a)=O⁡((log⁡n)3)\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi(2a),\mathsf{G}(a)}=O((\log n)^{3})

where the implicit constants in the asymptotic notation again depend on aa. Now a straightforward computation shows that Theorems 2.10 and 2.13 yield the desired results. ∎

Another result about graphs of subexponential growth that should be mentioned here is a theorem of Gao and Jackson [GJ15, Theorem 4.2] that asserts that for every d⩾2d\geqslant 2, the Schreier graph of the free part of the Bernoulli shift action ℤd↷{0,1}ℤd\mathbb{Z}^{d}\curvearrowright\{0,1\}^{\mathbb{Z}^{d}} admits a continuous proper 44-coloring. This fact can be alternatively derived by using Theorem 2.13 in combination with the deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm for 44-coloring grid graphs designed by Brandt et al. [Bra+17, Theorem 4].

3.E.  A pointwise version of the Abért–Weiss theorem

So far we have described a number of results in descriptive combinatorics that can be obtained using distributed algorithms. Now we present a direct application of the Measurable Symmetric LLL to a question in ergodic theory.

Throughout §3.E, Γ\Gamma shall denote a countably infinite group. We are interested in probability measure-preserving (p.m.p. ) actions of Γ\Gamma, i.e., actions of the form α:Γ↷(X,μ)\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright(X,\mu), where (X,μ)(X,\mu) is a standard probability space and the measure μ\mu is α\alpha-invariant. More generally, we consider Borel actions α:Γ↷X\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright X, i.e., actions of Γ\Gamma on a standard Borel space XX by Borel automorphisms. An action α:Γ↷X\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright X is free if the α\alpha-stabilizer of every point x∈Xx\in X is trivial.

An important example of a p.m.p. action is the Bernoulli shift action

σ:Γ↷([0,1]Γ,λΓ),\sigma\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright([0,1]^{\Gamma},\lambda^{\Gamma}),

where ([0,1],λ)([0,1],\lambda) is the unit interval equipped with the Lebesgue probability measure λ\lambda (owing to the measure isomorphism theorem [Kec95, Theorem 17.41], any other atomless standard probability space could be used instead). For brevity, we write

Ω≔[0,1]Γand𝝀≔λΓ\Omega\coloneqq[0,1]^{\Gamma}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\bm{\lambda}\coloneqq\lambda^{\Gamma}

(this notation will only be used in §3.E). Our starting point is a result of Abért and Weiss:

Theorem 3.19 (Abért–Weiss [AW13]).

Fix the following data:

  • —

    a partition Ω=A1⊔…⊔Ak\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k} of Ω\Omega into finitely many Borel pieces;

  • —

    a finite set F∈[Γ]<∞F\in[\Gamma]^{<\infty}; and

  • —

    ε>0\varepsilon>0.

For every free p.m.p. action α:Γ↷(X,μ)\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright(X,\mu), there is a Borel partition X=B1⊔…⊔BkX=B_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup B_{k} such that

μ(Bi∩γ⋅Bj)≈ε𝝀(Ai∩γ⋅Aj),\mu(B_{i}\cap\gamma\cdot B_{j})\,\approx_{\varepsilon}\,\bm{\lambda}(A_{i}\cap\gamma\cdot A_{j}),

for all 1⩽i1\leqslant i, j⩽kj\leqslant k and all γ∈F\gamma\in F.

Here and in what follows, we write a≈εba\approx_{\varepsilon}b to mean |a−b|<ε|a-b|<\varepsilon. Theorem 3.19 can be stated briefly as “The shift action σ:Γ↷(Ω,𝝀)\sigma\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright(\Omega,\bm{\lambda}) is weakly contained in every free p.m.p. action α:Γ↷(X,μ)\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright(X,\mu).” The relation of weak containment was introduced by Kechris in [Kec10, §10(C)]. For more details and further background on this topic, see the survey [BK20] by Burton and Kechris.

Here we strengthen Theorem 3.19 by replacing the quantities μ⁡(Bi∩γ⋅Bj)\mu(B_{i}\cap\gamma\cdot B_{j}) with certain pointwise averages almost everywhere:

Theorem 3.20.

Fix the following data:

  • —

    a partition Ω=A1⊔…⊔Ak\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k} of Ω\Omega into finitely many Borel pieces;

  • —

    a finite set F∈[Γ]<∞F\in[\Gamma]^{<\infty}; and

  • —

    ε>0\varepsilon>0.

Then there is n0∈ℕ+n_{0}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} with the following property. Fix a finite set D∈[Γ]<∞D\in[\Gamma]^{<\infty} of size |D|⩾n0|D|\geqslant n_{0} and let α:Γ↷X\alpha\colon\Gamma\curvearrowright X be a free Borel action of Γ\Gamma. For every probability Borel measure μ\mu on XX, there exists a Borel partition X=B1⊔…⊔BkX=B_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup B_{k} such that

(3.21) |{δ∈D:δ⋅x∈Bi∩γ⋅Bj}||D|≈ε𝝀(Ai∩γ⋅Aj),\frac{|\{\delta\in D\,:\,\delta\cdot x\in B_{i}\cap\gamma\cdot B_{j}\}|}{|D|}\,\approx_{\varepsilon}\,\bm{\lambda}(A_{i}\cap\gamma\cdot A_{j}),

for all 1⩽i1\leqslant i, j⩽kj\leqslant k, all γ∈F\gamma\in F, and μ\mu-almost all x∈Xx\in X.

Note that in Theorem 3.20, the measure μ\mu is not required to be α\alpha-invariant. If μ\mu is α\alpha-invariant, then the partition X=B1⊔…⊔BkX=B_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup B_{k} given by Theorem 3.20 also witnesses the conclusion of Theorem 3.19, as for an α\alpha-invariant measure μ\mu, we have

μ(Y)=∫X|{δ∈D:δ⋅x∈Y}||D|dμ(x),\mu(Y)\,=\,\int_{X}\frac{|\{\delta\in D\,:\,\delta\cdot x\in Y\}|}{|D|}\,\mathrm{d}\mu(x),

for all Borel Y⊆XY\subseteq X and any nonempty finite set D∈[Γ]<∞D\in[\Gamma]^{<\infty}. This shows that Theorem 3.20 is indeed a strengthening of Theorem 3.19. Statements in the spirit of Theorem 3.20 were first considered by the present author in [Ber20]. There, a weaker version of Theorem 3.20 was established, with (3.21) satisfied not for μ\mu-almost all x∈Xx\in X, but only on a set of x∈Xx\in X of measure at least 1−δ1-\delta, for any given δ>0\delta>0 [Ber20, Theorem 2.11]. The question of whether Theorem 3.20 is true was left there as an open problem [Ber20, Problem 8.2].

Proof of Theorem 3.20.

Only minimal modifications to the proof of [Ber20, Theorem 2.11] are needed to obtain Theorem 3.20. Specifically, in [Ber20, §§4.B and 7.A] the construction of a partition X=B1⊔…⊔BkX=B_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup B_{k} with the desired property is reduced to finding a measurable solution to a certain Borel CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} on XX. This CSP depends on the original partition Ω=A1⊔…⊔Ak\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k}, the finite set FF, the parameter ε\varepsilon, and the choice of the averaging set DD. It is immediate from the construction of ℬ\mathscr{B} that sup{|dom⁡(B)|:B∈ℬ}<∞\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}<\infty. Furthermore, the calculations given in the proof of [Ber20, Lemma 7.2] show that there exist positive reals aa, bb, and cc depending on the partition Ω=A1⊔…⊔Ak\Omega=A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{k}, the finite set FF, and the parameter ε\varepsilon but not on DD such that

(3.22) 𝗉⁡(ℬ)⩽a​exp⁡(−b​|D|)and𝖽⁡(ℬ)⩽c​|D|2−1.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\,\leqslant\,a\exp(-b|D|)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\,\leqslant\,c|D|^{2}-1.

At this point the proof of [Ber20, Theorem 2.11] invokes the approximate Symmetric LLL from [Ber19] (Theorem 6.5 in [Ber20]), which yields a measurable function that satisfies the constraints of the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} away from a set of measure less than δ\delta, for given δ>0\delta>0. To obtain Theorem 3.20, we instead use Theorem 2.20. By (3.22),

𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽a​exp⁡(−b​|D|)⋅c8​|D|16.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,a\exp(-b|D|)\cdot c^{8}|D|^{16}.

The latter quantity approaches 00 as |D|→∞|D|\to\infty; in particular, it is less than 2−152^{-15} whenever |D||D| is large enough. Hence, by Theorem 2.20, assuming |D||D| is sufficiently large, the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} has a measurable solution, and we are done. ∎

4.  Using distributed algorithms

4.A.  Proof of Theorem 2.10

We start with the following simple observation, which will be used repeatedly throughout §§4 and 5:

Lemma 4.1.

If 𝑮\bm{G} is a locally finite Borel structured graph, then the function

V⁡(𝑮)×ℕ→𝖥𝖲𝖦∙:(x,R)↦[B𝑮​(x,R),x]V(\bm{G})\times{\mathbb{N}}\to\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\colon(x,R)\mapsto[B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x]

is Borel (here 𝖥𝖲𝖦∙\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet} is viewed as a discrete countable space).

Proof.

We need to argue that for every finite rooted structured graph (𝑯,v)(\bm{H},v), the set

(4.2) {(x,R)∈V⁡(𝑮)×ℕ:(B𝑮​(x,R),x)≅(𝑯,v)}\{(x,R)\in V(\bm{G})\times{\mathbb{N}}\,:\,(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x)\cong(\bm{H},v)\}

is Borel. Since 𝑮\bm{G} is locally finite, by the Feldman–Moore theorem [KM04, Theorem 1.3], there exist Borel involutions γi:V⁡(𝑮)→V⁡(𝑮)\gamma_{i}\colon V(\bm{G})\to V(\bm{G}), i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, such that dist𝑮​(x,y)<∞{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)<\infty if and only if y=γi​(x)y=\gamma_{i}(x) for some i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}. Without loss of generality, we may assume that γ0\gamma_{0} is the identity map on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}). For all xx, y∈V⁡(𝑮)y\in V(\bm{G}) such that dist𝑮​(x,y)<∞{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)<\infty, let 𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗑⁡(x,y)\mathsf{index}(x,y) denote the minimum i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}} with γi​(x)=y\gamma_{i}(x)=y (in particular, 𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗑⁡(x,x)=0\mathsf{index}(x,x)=0). Now, for any x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}) and R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, we have that (B𝑮​(x,R),x)≅(𝑯,v)(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x)\cong(\bm{H},v) if and only if there exists a partial function φ∈[ℕ⇀V(𝑯)]<∞\varphi\in[{\mathbb{N}}\rightharpoonup V(\bm{H})]^{<\infty} such that:

  • —

    φ\varphi is a bijection between dom⁡(φ)∈[ℕ]<∞\mathrm{dom}(\varphi)\in[{\mathbb{N}}]^{<\infty} and V⁡(𝑯)V(\bm{H});

  • —

    for all i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, we have i∈dom⁡(φ)i\in\mathrm{dom}(\varphi) if and only if dist𝑮​(x,γi​(x))⩽R{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,\gamma_{i}(x))\leqslant R and i=𝗂𝗇𝖽𝖾𝗑⁡(x,γi​(x))i=\mathsf{index}(x,\gamma_{i}(x));

  • —

    the mapping γi​(x)↦φ​(i)\gamma_{i}(x)\mapsto\varphi(i) is an isomorphism of the structured graphs B𝑮​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R) and 𝑯\bm{H};

  • —

    φ⁡(0)=v\varphi(0)=v.

Since the set [ℕ⇀V(𝑯)]<∞[{\mathbb{N}}\rightharpoonup V(\bm{H})]^{<\infty} is countable, it follows that the set (4.2) is a countable union of Borel sets (one for each φ∈[ℕ⇀V(𝑯)]<∞\varphi\in[{\mathbb{N}}\rightharpoonup V(\bm{H})]^{<\infty}), and hence it is itself Borel. ∎

A useful consequence of Lemma 4.1 is that if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm and 𝑮\bm{G} is a locally finite Borel structured graph, then for each T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, the map 𝒜⁡(𝑮,T):V⁡(𝑮)→ℕ\mathcal{A}(\bm{G},T)\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} is Borel. We will make extensive use of this observation throughout the remainder of the paper.

After these preliminary remarks, we are ready to prove Theorem 2.10.

Proof of Theorem 2.10.

Our proof of Theorem 2.10 is similar to the argument used by Chang, Kopelowitz, and Pettie to prove that no local coloring problem has deterministic 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity in the range ω⁡(log∗⁡n)\omega(\log^{\ast}n) and o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) [CKP19, Corollary 3]. Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that T≔𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)T\coloneqq\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) is finite and let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm witnessing the bound 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T. Set R≔T+tR\coloneqq T+t. Now let 𝑮\bm{G} be a Borel structured graph that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}). Our goal is to show that 𝑮\bm{G} has a Borel Π\Pi-coloring. To this end, let G′G^{\prime} be the graph with V⁡(G′)≔V⁡(𝑮)V(G^{\prime})\coloneqq V(\bm{G}) in which two distinct vertices xx, yy are adjacent if and only if dist𝑮​(x,y)⩽2​R{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)\leqslant 2R. The graph G′G^{\prime} is Borel and satisfies Δ⁡(G′)=sup{|B𝑮​(x,2​R)|−1:x∈V⁡(G)}⩽n−1\Delta(G^{\prime})=\sup\{|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|-1\,:\,x\in V(G)\}\leqslant n-1 (we are subtracting 11 since a vertex is never adjacent to itself). Hence, by the Kechris–Solecki–Todorcevic Theorem 3.1, G′G^{\prime} has a Borel proper coloring c:V⁡(𝑮)→[n]c\colon V(\bm{G})\to[n]. Define a function f:V⁡(𝑮)→ℕf\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} by f≔𝒜⁡(𝑮c,T)f\coloneqq\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{c},T). The function ff is Borel, and we claim that it is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}. In other words, we claim that

𝒫⁡(𝑮f,t)​(x)= 1for all ​x∈V⁡(𝑮).\mathcal{P}(\bm{G}_{f},t)(x)\,=\,1\quad\text{for all }x\in V(\bm{G}).

Fix any x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}). Since 𝑮\bm{G} is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G}, there exist an nn-vertex structured graph 𝑯\bm{H} with [𝑯]∈𝖦[\bm{H}]\in\mathsf{G} and a vertex y∈V⁡(𝑯)y\in V(\bm{H}) such that [B𝑮​(x,R),x]=[B𝑯​(y,R),y][B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x]=[B_{\bm{H}}(y,R),y]. Let φ\varphi be an isomorphism between B𝑯​(y,R)B_{\bm{H}}(y,R) and B𝑮​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R) sending yy to xx. Notice that the vertices of B𝑮​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R) are pairwise adjacent in G′G^{\prime}, so they are assigned distinct colors by cc. Hence, we can extend the function c∘φc\circ\varphi to a bijection 𝗂𝖽:V⁡(𝑯)→[n]\mathsf{id}\colon V(\bm{H})\to[n]. Since 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm witnessing the bound 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T, the function g≔𝒜⁡(𝑯𝗂𝖽,T)g\coloneqq\mathcal{A}(\bm{H}_{\mathsf{id}},T) is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑯\bm{H}. In particular,

𝒫​(𝑯g,t)​(y)= 1.\mathcal{P}(\bm{H}_{g},t)(y)\,=\,1.

It remains to observe that the tt-ball around xx in 𝑮f\bm{G}_{f} is isomorphic to the tt-ball around yy in 𝑯g\bm{H}_{g}, and hence 𝒫⁡(𝑮f,t)​(x)=𝒫⁡(𝑯g,t)​(y)=1\mathcal{P}(\bm{G}_{f},t)(x)=\mathcal{P}(\bm{H}_{g},t)(y)=1, as desired. ∎

4.B.  Proof of Theorem 2.13

The proof of Theorem 2.13 is virtually the same as the proof of Theorem 2.10 given in §4.A. We just have to make sure that the construction described there produces a continuous coloring. To this end, we start with a few simple observations about topological graphs. First, it is an immediate consequence of Definition 2.12 that if 𝑮\bm{G} is a topological graph, then the function

V⁡(𝑮)×ℕ→𝖥𝖲𝖦∙:(x,R)↦[B𝑮​(x,R),x]V(\bm{G})\times{\mathbb{N}}\to\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet}\colon(x,R)\mapsto[B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x]

is continuous (here the countable set 𝖥𝖲𝖦∙\mathsf{FSG}_{\bullet} is viewed as a discrete space). In particular, this implies that if 𝒜\mathcal{A} is a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm and 𝑮\bm{G} is a topological structured graph, then for each T∈ℕT\in{\mathbb{N}}, the map 𝒜⁡(𝑮,T):V⁡(𝑮)→ℕ\mathcal{A}(\bm{G},T)\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} is continuous. Next, we shall need the following fact:

Lemma 4.3.

Let 𝑮\bm{G} be a topological structured graph. If f:V⁡(𝑮)→ℕf\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} is a continuous function, then 𝑮f\bm{G}_{f} is also a topological structured graph.

Proof.

Let dd be a metric inducing the topology on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}). Fix x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), R∈ℕR\in{\mathbb{N}}, and ε>0\varepsilon>0. Since 𝑮\bm{G} is locally finite, we have |B𝑮​(x,R)|<∞|B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)|<\infty, and hence, by making ε\varepsilon smaller if necessary, we may arrange that ff is constant on the ε\varepsilon-neighborhood of each vertex z∈V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R))z\in V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)). Since 𝑮\bm{G} is a topological structured graph, there is δ>0\delta>0 be such that for every yy in the δ\delta-neighborhood of xx, the rooted structured graphs (B𝑮​(x,R),x)(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x) and (B𝑮​(y,R),y)(B_{\bm{G}}(y,R),y) are ε\varepsilon-isomorphic. Let φ\varphi be an isomorphism between (B𝑮​(x,R),x)(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x) and (B𝑮​(y,R),y)(B_{\bm{G}}(y,R),y) such that d⁡(z,φ⁡(z))<εd(z,\varphi(z))<\varepsilon for all z∈V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R))z\in V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)). Then, by the assumption on ε\varepsilon, f⁡(z)=f⁡(φ⁡(z))f(z)=f(\varphi(z)) for all z∈V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R))z\in V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)) as well, so the rooted structured graphs (B𝑮f​(x,R),x)(B_{\bm{G}_{f}}(x,R),x) and (B𝑮f​(y,R),y)(B_{\bm{G}_{f}}(y,R),y) are ε\varepsilon-isomorphic, as desired. ∎

We also require a couple results about continuous colorings of topological graphs.

Lemma 4.4.

If GG is a topological graph, then GG admits a continuous proper coloring c:V⁡(G)→ℕc\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}}.

Proof.

Since V⁡(G)V(G) is a zero-dimensional Polish space, there is a countable base (Ui)i=0∞(U_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} for the topology on V⁡(G)V(G) consisting of clopen sets. For each i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, define a set Vi⊆V⁡(G)V_{i}\subseteq V(G) by setting

x∈Vi:⟺x∈Ui​ and ​NG​(x)∩Ui=∅.x\in V_{i}\quad\vcentcolon\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in U_{i}\text{ and }N_{G}(x)\cap U_{i}=\varnothing.

By construction, each set ViV_{i} is independent in GG (i.e., no two vertices in ViV_{i} are adjacent). Since (Ui)i=0∞(U_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} is a base for the topology on V⁡(G)V(G) and GG is locally finite, for each x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) there is some i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}} such that x∈Vix\in V_{i}. In other words, V⁡(G)=⋃i=0∞ViV(G)=\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}V_{i}. Note that whether or not x∈Vix\in V_{i} is determined by the isomorphism type of the rooted radius-11 ball around xx in the structured graph (G,1Ui)(G,1_{U_{i}}), where 1Ui:V⁡(G)→{0,1}1_{U_{i}}\colon V(G)\to\{0,1\} is the indicator function of UiU_{i}. Since UiU_{i} is clopen, 1Ui1_{U_{i}} is continuous, so (G,1Ui)(G,1_{U_{i}}) is a topological structured graph, and hence the set ViV_{i} is clopen as well. To summarize, we have expressed V⁡(G)V(G) as a countable union of clopen sets that are independent in GG. Now define Wi≔Vi∖⋃j=0i−1VjW_{i}\coloneqq V_{i}\setminus\bigcup_{j=0}^{i-1}V_{j}. The sets WiW_{i} are again clopen, independent in GG, and satisfy V⁡(G)=⋃i=0∞WiV(G)=\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}W_{i}. Additionally, they are pairwise disjoint. Thus, we may define a function c:V⁡(G)→ℕc\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} via

c⁡(x)=i:⟺x∈Wi.c(x)=i\quad\vcentcolon\Longleftrightarrow\quad x\in W_{i}.

This cc is a desired continuous proper coloring. ∎

Lemma 4.5.

If GG is a topological graph of finite maximum degree Δ\Delta, then GG admits a continuous proper coloring c:V⁡(G)→[Δ+1]c\colon V(G)\to[\Delta+1].

Proof.

Let r:V⁡(G)→ℕr\colon V(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} be a continuous proper coloring of GG that exists by Lemma 4.4. For each i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, set Wi≔r−1​(i)W_{i}\coloneqq r^{-1}(i) and define functions ci:Wi→[Δ+1]c_{i}\colon W_{i}\to[\Delta+1] recursively by

ci​(x)≔min⁡{j∈[Δ+1]:there is no y∈NG​(x) with r⁡(y)<i and cr⁡(y)​(y)=j}.c_{i}(x)\,\coloneqq\,\min\{j\in[\Delta+1]\,:\,\text{there is no $y\in N_{G}(x)$ with $r(y)<i$ and $c_{r(y)}(y)=j$}\}.

The fact that |NG​(x)|⩽Δ|N_{G}(x)|\leqslant\Delta for all x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) ensures that ci​(x)c_{i}(x) is well-defined. Set c≔⋃i=0∞cic\coloneqq\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}c_{i}. By construction, cc is a proper (Δ+1)(\Delta+1)-coloring of GG. It remains to observe that cc is continuous, since for each x∈Wix\in W_{i}, the value c⁡(x)c(x) is determined by the isomorphism type of the rooted radius-ii ball around xx in the topological structured graph GrG_{r}. ∎

Now we can easily verify that the construction from §4.A produces a continuous coloring. Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that T≔𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)<∞T\coloneqq\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)<\infty and let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm witnessing the inequality 𝖣𝖾𝗍Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Det}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T. Set R≔T+tR\coloneqq T+t. Let 𝑮\bm{G} be a topological structured graph that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}). Define G′G^{\prime} to be the graph with V⁡(G′)≔V⁡(𝑮)V(G^{\prime})\coloneqq V(\bm{G}) in which two distinct vertices xx, yy are adjacent if and only if dist𝑮​(x,y)⩽2​R{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)\leqslant 2R. It is clear that G′G^{\prime} is a topological graph of maximum degree at most n−1n-1, so, by Lemma 4.5, G′G^{\prime} has a continuous proper coloring c:V⁡(𝑮)→[n]c\colon V(\bm{G})\to[n]. Define a function f:V⁡(𝑮)→ℕf\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} by f≔𝒜⁡(𝑮c,T)f\coloneqq\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{c},T). Since 𝑮c\bm{G}_{c} is a topological structured graph, ff is continuous, and the argument from §4.A shows that ff is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}, as desired.

4.C.  Reduction from randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithms to the LLL

Recall that a CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is called bounded if sup{|dom⁡(B)|:B∈ℬ}<∞\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}<\infty (this is one of the assumptions in Theorem 2.20). The main result of this section is the following lemma:

Lemma 4.6.

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that T≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)T\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) is finite and set R≔T+tR\coloneqq T+t. Let m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} witness the bound 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T. If 𝑮\bm{G} is a Borel structured graph of finite maximum degree that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G}, then there exists a bounded Borel CSP ℬ:V(𝑮)→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon V(\bm{G})\to^{?}[m] such that:

  1. (i)

    for every solution ϑ:V⁡(𝑮)→[m]\vartheta\colon V(\bm{G})\to[m] to ℬ\mathscr{B}, the function 𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T)\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T) is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G};

  2. (ii)

    𝗉⁡(ℬ)⩽1/n\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant 1/n and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)⩽sup{|B𝑮​(x,2​R)|−1:x∈V⁡(𝑮)}\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant\sup\{|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|-1\,:\,x\in V(\bm{G})\}.

Proof.

For each ϑ:V⁡(𝑮)→[m]\vartheta\colon V(\bm{G})\to[m], let fϑ≔𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T)f_{\vartheta}\coloneqq\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T). Note that for every x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}), the value 𝒫​(𝑮fϑ,t)​(x)\mathcal{P}(\bm{G}_{f_{\vartheta}},t)(x) is determined by the isomorphism type of the rooted RR-ball around xx in 𝑮ϑ\bm{G}_{\vartheta}. Therefore, we may define a set BxB_{x} of functions φ:V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R))→[m]\varphi\colon V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R))\to[m] via

φ∈Bx:⟺𝒫⁡(𝑮fϑ,t)​(x)=0​ for some (hence all) ​ϑ:V⁡(𝑮)→[m]​ such that ​ϑ⊇φ.\varphi\in B_{x}\quad\vcentcolon\Longleftrightarrow\quad\mathcal{P}(\bm{G}_{f_{\vartheta}},t)(x)=0\text{ for some {(}hence all{)} }\vartheta\colon V(\bm{G})\to[m]\text{ such that }\vartheta\supseteq\varphi.

Each BxB_{x} is a (V⁡(𝑮),m)(V(\bm{G}),m)-constraint such that either dom⁡(Bx)=V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R))\mathrm{dom}(B_{x})=V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)) or Bx=∅B_{x}=\varnothing. Let

ℬ≔{Bx:x∈V⁡(𝑮)}.\mathscr{B}\,\coloneqq\,\{B_{x}\,:\,x\in V(\bm{G})\}.

Then ℬ\mathscr{B} is a Borel CSP on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}) with range [m][m], and we claim that it has all the desired properties. Since the maximum degree of 𝑮\bm{G} is finite, ℬ\mathscr{B} is bounded. The definition of each constraint BxB_{x} implies that if ϑ|dom⁡(Bx)∉Bx{{\vartheta}|{\mathrm{dom}(B_{x})}}\not\in B_{x}, then 𝒫​(𝑮fϑ,t)​(x)=1\mathcal{P}(\bm{G}_{f_{\vartheta}},t)(x)=1, and therefore (i) holds. The bound

𝖽⁡(ℬ)⩽sup{|B𝑮​(x,2​R)|−1:x∈V⁡(𝑮)}\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\,\leqslant\,\sup\{|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|-1\,:\,x\in V(\bm{G})\}

follows from the observation that if By∈N⁡(Bx)B_{y}\in\mathrm{N}(B_{x}), then V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R))∩V⁡(B𝑮​(y,R))≠∅V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R))\cap V(B_{\bm{G}}(y,R))\neq\varnothing and thus dist𝑮​(x,y)⩽2​R{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)\leqslant 2R. (Here we are subtracting 11 because dist𝑮​(x,x)⩽2​R{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,x)\leqslant 2R but Bx∉N⁡(Bx)B_{x}\not\in\mathrm{N}(B_{x}).) It remains to verify that 𝗉⁡(ℬ)⩽1/n\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant 1/n. To this end, fix a vertex x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}). We wish to show that ℙ⁡[Bx]⩽1/n\mathbb{P}[B_{x}]\leqslant 1/n. Since 𝑮\bm{G} is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G}, there exist an nn-vertex structured graph 𝑯\bm{H} with [𝑯]∈𝖦[\bm{H}]\in\mathsf{G} and a vertex y∈V⁡(𝑯)y\in V(\bm{H}) such that [B𝑮​(x,R),x]=[B𝑯​(y,R),y][B_{\bm{G}}(x,R),x]=[B_{\bm{H}}(y,R),y]. To simplify the notation we assume, without loss of generality, that x=yx=y and B𝑮​(x,R)=B𝑯​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)=B_{\bm{H}}(x,R). Pick a function ϑ:V⁡(𝑯)→[m]\vartheta\colon V(\bm{H})\to[m] uniformly at random and define g≔𝒜⁡(𝑯ϑ,T)g\coloneqq\mathcal{A}(\bm{H}_{\vartheta},T) and φ≔ϑ|dom⁡(Bx)\varphi\coloneqq{{\vartheta}|{\mathrm{dom}(B_{x})}} (thus, gg and φ\varphi are also random functions). By the construction of BxB_{x} and since B𝑮​(x,R)=B𝑯​(x,R)B_{\bm{G}}(x,R)=B_{\bm{H}}(x,R), if φ∈Bx\varphi\in B_{x}, then 𝒫​(𝑯g,t)​(x)=0\mathcal{P}(\bm{H}_{g},t)(x)=0 and, in particular, gg is not a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑯\bm{H}. Therefore,

ℙ[Bx]=ℙ[φ∈Bx]⩽ℙ[g is not a Π-coloring of 𝑯]⩽1n,\mathbb{P}[B_{x}]\,=\,\mathbb{P}[\varphi\in B_{x}]\,\leqslant\,\mathbb{P}[\text{$g$ is not a $\Pi$-coloring of $\bm{H}$}]\,\leqslant\,\frac{1}{n},

where the last inequality holds since 𝒜\mathcal{A} witnesses the bound 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T. ∎

Next we apply Lemma 4.6 to derive Theorem 2.14 from the Measurable Symmetric LLL. For technical reasons, a somewhat stronger version of the Measurable Symmetric LLL is required:

Theorem 2.20′.

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a bounded Borel CSP such that

𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽ 2−15.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2^{-15}.

Then the following conclusions hold:

  1. (i)

    If ℳ\mathcal{M} is a countable set of probability Borel measures on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution that is simultaneously μ\mu-measurable for all μ∈ℳ\mu\in\mathcal{M}.

  2. (ii)

    If 𝒯\mathcal{T} is a countable set of compatible Polish topologies on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a solution that is simultaneously τ\tau-Baire-measurable for all τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}.

While it appears more general, Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C(i) is actually an easy consequence of Theorem 2.20(i). Indeed, if ℳ={μn:n∈ℕ}\mathcal{M}=\{\mu_{n}\,:\,n\in{\mathbb{N}}\} is a countable set of probability Borel measures on XX, then the conclusion of Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C(i) is obtained by applying Theorem 2.20(i) to the measure μ≔∑n=0∞2−n−1​μn\mu\coloneqq\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}2^{-n-1}\mu_{n}. On the other hand, Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C(ii) requires an independent argument, which we give in §5.F.

Proof of Theorem 2.14 assuming Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C.

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that T≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)T\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) is finite and set R≔T+tR\coloneqq T+t. Let m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} witness the bound 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T. Let 𝑮\bm{G} be a Borel structured graph that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that

|B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n1/8/4for all ​x∈V⁡(𝑮).|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n^{1/8}/4\quad\text{for all }x\in V(\bm{G}).

Given a Borel probability measure μ\mu on V⁡(𝑮)V(\bm{G}), we wish to find a μ\mu-measurable Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G} (the argument for Baire-measurable colorings is the same, mutatis mutandis). By the Feldman–Moore theorem [KM04, Theorem 1.3], there exist Borel involutions γi:V⁡(𝑮)→V⁡(𝑮)\gamma_{i}\colon V(\bm{G})\to V(\bm{G}), i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, such that dist𝑮​(x,y)<∞{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)<\infty if and only if y=γi​(x)y=\gamma_{i}(x) for some i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}. Define

ℳ≔{(γi)∗​(μ):i∈ℕ}.\mathcal{M}\,\coloneqq\,\{(\gamma_{i})_{\ast}(\mu)\,:\,i\in{\mathbb{N}}\}.

Letting ℬ:V(𝑮)→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon V(\bm{G})\to^{?}[m] be a Borel CSP given by Lemma 4.6, we have

𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)8⩽1n⋅(n1/8/4)8= 2−16.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,\frac{1}{n}\cdot(n^{1/8}/4)^{8}\,=\,2^{-16}.

Therefore, we may apply Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C(i) to obtain a solution ϑ:V⁡(𝑮)→ℕ\vartheta\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} to ℬ\mathscr{B} that is measurable with respect to every measure (γi)∗​(μ)(\gamma_{i})_{\ast}(\mu). This means that ϑ\vartheta agrees with a Borel function away from a set S⊆V⁡(𝑮)S\subseteq V(\bm{G}) that is (γi)∗​(μ)(\gamma_{i})_{\ast}(\mu)-null for all i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}. Let S′S^{\prime} be the 𝑮\bm{G}-saturation of SS, i.e., the set of all the vertices of 𝑮\bm{G} whose distance to an element of SS is finite. Then the set S′S^{\prime} is 𝑮\bm{G}-invariant, i.e., no edges of 𝑮\bm{G} join S′S^{\prime} to V⁡(G)∖S′V(G)\setminus S^{\prime}. Notice that S′=⋃n=0∞γi​(S)S^{\prime}=\bigcup_{n=0}^{\infty}\gamma_{i}(S), and hence

μ⁡(S′)⩽∑n=0∞μ⁡(γi​(S))=∑n=0∞((γi)∗​(μ))​(S)= 0.\mu(S^{\prime})\,\leqslant\,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\mu(\gamma_{i}(S))\,=\,\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}((\gamma_{i})_{\ast}(\mu))(S)\,=\,0.

Since ϑ\vartheta is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}, 𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T)\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T) is a Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}. Also, since ϑ\vartheta agrees with a Borel function away from S′S^{\prime} and S′S^{\prime} is 𝑮\bm{G}-invariant, we conclude that so does 𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T)\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T). The set S′S^{\prime} is μ\mu-null, so this implies that 𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T)\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T) is μ\mu-measurable, as desired. ∎

We can use Lemma 4.6 in a similar fashion to prove Theorem 2.15. Instead of Theorem 2.20, this argument involves the subexponential Borel LLL of Csóka, Grabowski, Máthé, Pikhurko, and Tyros:

Theorem 4.7 (Csóka–Grabowski–Máthé–Pikhurko–Tyros [Csó+22]).

Let GG be a Borel graph of subexponential growth. Fix m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and assign to each vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) a set BxB_{x} of functions from V​(BG​(x,1))V(B_{G}(x,1)) to [m][m]. Viewing every BxB_{x} as a (V⁡(G),m)(V(G),m)-constraint, form a CSP ℬ≔{Bx:x∈V⁡(G)}\mathscr{B}\coloneqq\{B_{x}\,:\,x\in V(G)\}. Suppose that the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is Borel. If

𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅sup{|BG​(x,2)|:x∈V⁡(G)}⩽e−1,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot\sup\{|B_{G}(x,2)|\,:\,x\in V(G)\}\,\leqslant\,e^{-1},

then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel solution.

Proof of Theorem 2.15.

Let Π=(t,𝒫)\Pi=(t,\mathcal{P}) be a local coloring problem and let 𝖦⊆𝖥𝖲𝖦\mathsf{G}\subseteq\mathsf{FSG}. Fix n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} such that T≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)T\coloneqq\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n) is finite and set R≔T+tR\coloneqq T+t. Let m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜\mathcal{A} witness the bound 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽Π,𝖦​(n)⩽T\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi,\mathsf{G}}(n)\leqslant T. Let 𝑮\bm{G} be a Borel structured graph of subexponential growth that is (R,n)(R,n)-locally in 𝖦\mathsf{G} and such that |B𝑮​(x,2​R)|⩽n/e|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\leqslant n/e for all x∈V⁡(𝑮)x\in V(\bm{G}). We wish to find a Borel Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}. To this end, let ℬ:V(𝑮)→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon V(\bm{G})\to^{?}[m] be a Borel CSP given by Lemma 4.6 and let G′G^{\prime} be the graph with V⁡(G′)≔V⁡(𝑮)V(G^{\prime})\coloneqq V(\bm{G}) in which two distinct vertices xx, yy are adjacent if and only if dist𝑮​(x,y)⩽R{\mathrm{dist}}_{\bm{G}}(x,y)\leqslant R. It is straightforward to verify that the construction of ℬ\mathscr{B} presented in the proof of Lemma 4.6 fulfills the requirements of Theorem 4.7 with the role of GG played by G′G^{\prime}. Furthermore,

𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅sup{|BG′​(x,2)|:x∈V⁡(G′)}=𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅sup{|B𝑮​(x,2​R)|:x∈V⁡(𝑮)}⩽1n⋅ne=e−1.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot\sup\{|B_{G^{\prime}}(x,2)|\,:\,x\in V(G^{\prime})\}\,=\,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot\sup\{|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R)|\,:\,x\in V(\bm{G})\}\,\leqslant\,\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{n}{e}\,=\,e^{-1}.

Since G′G^{\prime} is a Borel graph of subexponential growth, Theorem 4.7 yields a Borel solution ϑ:V⁡(𝑮)→ℕ\vartheta\colon V(\bm{G})\to{\mathbb{N}} to ℬ\mathscr{B}. Then 𝒜⁡(𝑮ϑ,T)\mathcal{A}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T) is a Borel Π\Pi-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}, and we are done. ∎

5.  Proof of the Measurable Symmetric LLL

5.A.  Proof outline

In this section we outline our strategy for proving Theorem 2.20. Say that ℬ\mathscr{B} is an (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP if

𝗉⁡(ℬ)⋅(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)N⩽ε.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{N}\,\leqslant\,\varepsilon.

We shall describe here the main steps in proving that Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSPs have measurable solutions; the Baire-measurable case is similar but differs in some technical aspects.

An important role in our argument is played by the notion of a reduction between CSPs. Roughly speaking, a CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is reducible to a CSP 𝒞\mathscr{C} if there is a “local rule” that transforms any solution to 𝒞\mathscr{C} into a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}; thus, to solve ℬ\mathscr{B}, it suffices to solve 𝒞\mathscr{C}. The precise definition of what we mean by a “local rule” here is given in Definitions 5.1 and 5.4; it has some similarities and is closely related to the notion of a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm. The first key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 2.20 is a “bootstrapping lemma” (Lemma 5.11), which asserts that if ℬ\mathscr{B} is an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP, then ℬ\mathscr{B} is reducible to an (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP 𝒞\mathscr{C} for any N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0. The proof of this fact involves the bootstrapping technique developed by Fischer and Ghaffari in [FG17, §3.2], which in turn is based on the work of Chang and Pettie [CP19] on the randomized time hierarchy for the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model. A CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} can be interpreted as a local coloring problem on an auxiliary graph (see §5.D for details). Ghaffari, Harris, and Kuhn [GHK18] showed that if ℬ\mathscr{B} is an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP, then the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of the corresponding local coloring problem is o⁡(log⁡n)o(\log n) (the work of Ghaffari, Harris, and Kuhn builds on the earlier breakthrough of Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] who obtained the same conclusion for (32,e−32)(32,e^{-32})-CSPs). Our “bootstrapping lemma” follows by combining the Ghaffari–Harris–Kuhn result with Lemma 4.6.

Next we need to discuss partial solutions to CSPs. Given a CSP ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m], a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} is a partial map g:X⇀[m]g\colon X\rightharpoonup[m] that can be extended to a full solution f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m]. Given a partial solution gg to ℬ\mathscr{B}, the problem of extending gg to a full solution can naturally be encoded as a CSP on X∖dom⁡(g)X\setminus\mathrm{dom}(g); we denote this CSP by ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g (see §5.C for the definition). The second key ingredient in our proof is Lemma 5.12, which says, roughly, that if NN and 1/ε1/\varepsilon are large enough and ℬ\mathscr{B} is a Borel (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP on a standard probability space (X,μ)(X,\mu), then ℬ\mathscr{B} has a Borel partial solution gg such that dom⁡(g)\mathrm{dom}(g) has measure at least, say, 1/21/2 and the CSP ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g satisfies 𝗉⁡(ℬ/g)⪅𝗉⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}/g)\lessapprox\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})}. Arguments similar to Lemma 5.12 have been used by Fischer and Ghaffari [FG17] and Molloy and Reed [MR98] and ultimately go back to the seminal work of Beck [Bec91].

Now we can sketch the overall flow of the proof. We are given a Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} on a standard probability space (X,μ)(X,\mu). Using Lemma 5.11, we “bootstrap” ℬ\mathscr{B} to an (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP, where NN, 1/ε≫11/\varepsilon\gg 1. We then apply Lemma 5.12 to get a Borel partial solution g0g_{0} to ℬ\mathscr{B} such that μ⁡(dom⁡(g0))⩾1/2\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g_{0}))\geqslant 1/2 and 𝗉⁡(ℬ/g0)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B}/g_{0}) is still very small; in particular, by making NN and 1/ε1/\varepsilon sufficiently large, we may arrange ℬ/g0\mathscr{B}/g_{0} to be reducible to an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP (see Lemma 5.18). We then repeat the same steps with ℬ/g0\mathscr{B}/g_{0} in place of ℬ\mathscr{B} and obtain a Borel partial solution g1g_{1} to ℬ/g0\mathscr{B}/g_{0} such that μ⁡(dom⁡(g1))⩾(1−μ⁡(dom⁡(g0)))/2\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g_{1}))\geqslant(1-\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g_{0})))/2 and ℬ/(g0∪g1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup g_{1}) is again reducible to an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP. After countably many such iterations, we will have constructed a sequence g0g_{0}, g1g_{1}, … of Borel functions such that g≔g0∪g1∪…g\coloneqq g_{0}\cup g_{1}\cup\ldots is a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} with μ⁡(dom⁡(g))=1\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g))=1. Since gg is a partial solution, it can be extended to a full solution ff, and any such ff is μ\mu-measurable, as desired.

5.B.  Reductions between CSPs

For sets AA and BB, we use [A⇀B][A\rightharpoonup B] to denote the set of all partial functions A⇀BA\rightharpoonup B. For functions ff, gg, the notation g⊆fg\subseteq f means that ff is an extension of gg, i.e., dom⁡(g)⊆dom⁡(f)\mathrm{dom}(g)\subseteq\mathrm{dom}(f) and g=f|dom⁡(g)g={{f}|{\mathrm{dom}(g)}}. The following definitions are crucial for our proof of Theorem 2.20.

Definition 5.1 (Connections).

An (X,Y)(X,Y)-connection, where XX and YY are sets, is a mapping ρ:[Y⇀ℕ]→[X⇀ℕ]\rho\colon[Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}]\to[X\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}] that is monotone in the sense that if f:Y⇀ℕf\colon Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} and g⊆fg\subseteq f, then ρ⁡(g)⊆ρ⁡(f)\rho(g)\subseteq\rho(f) as well. We say that a set S⊆YS\subseteq Y ρ\rho-determines an element x∈Xx\in X if for all f:Y⇀ℕf\colon Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}},

(5.2) ρ⁡(f)​(x)=ρ⁡(f|S)​(x).\rho(f)(x)\,=\,\rho({{f}|{S}})(x).

When one side of (5.2) is undefined, we interpret the equality to mean that the other side is undefined as well. The width of an (X,Y)(X,Y)-connection ρ\rho is the quantity

𝗐⁡(ρ)≔supx∈Xinf{|S|:S⊆Y is a set that ρ-determines x}.\mathsf{w}(\rho)\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{x\in X}\,\inf\{|S|\,:\,\text{$S\subseteq Y$ is a set that $\rho$-determines $x$}\}.

An (X,Y)(X,Y)-connection ρ\rho is local if 𝗐⁡(ρ)\mathsf{w}(\rho) is finite.

Lemma/Definition 5.3 (Sρ​(x)S_{\rho}(x)).

Let ρ\rho be a local (X,Y)(X,Y)-connection. Then for each x∈Xx\in X, there is a unique set Sρ​(x)⊆YS_{\rho}(x)\subseteq Y such that S⊆YS\subseteq Y ρ\rho-determines xx if and only if S⊇Sρ​(x)S\supseteq S_{\rho}(x).

Proof.

This is a consequence of the fact that if S1S_{1}, S2⊆YS_{2}\subseteq Y are sets that ρ\rho-determine xx, then S1∩S2S_{1}\cap S_{2} also ρ\rho-determines xx, which holds since for any f:Y⇀ℕf\colon Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}},

ρ⁡(f)​(x)=ρ⁡(f|S1)​(x)=ρ⁡((f|S1)|S2)​(x)=ρ⁡(f|(S1∩S2))​(x).∎\rho(f)(x)\,=\,\rho({{f}|{S_{1}}})(x)\,=\,\rho({{({{f}|{S_{1}}})}|{S_{2}}})(x)\,=\,\rho({{f}|{(S_{1}\cap S_{2})}})(x).\qed
Definition 5.4 (Reductions).

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] and 𝒞:Y→?[n]\mathscr{C}\colon Y\to^{?}[n] be CSPs. A reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to 𝒞\mathscr{C} is a local (X,Y)(X,Y)-connection ρ\rho such that for all f:Y→[n]f\colon Y\to[n],

f is a solution to 𝒞⟹ρ⁡(f) is a solution to ℬ.\text{$f$ is a solution to $\mathscr{C}$}\quad\Longrightarrow\quad\text{$\rho(f)$ is a solution to $\mathscr{B}$}.

The degree of a reduction ρ\rho is the quantity

𝖽⁡(ρ)≔supx∈X|{C∈𝒞:dom⁡(C)∩Sρ​(x)≠∅}|.\mathsf{d}(\rho)\,\coloneqq\,\sup_{x\in X}\,|\{C\in\mathscr{C}\,:\,\mathrm{dom}(C)\cap S_{\rho}(x)\neq\varnothing\}|.

If there is a reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to 𝒞\mathscr{C}, then we say that ℬ\mathscr{B} is reducible to 𝒞\mathscr{C} and write ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} to indicate that ρ\rho is a reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to 𝒞\mathscr{C}. Note that every reduction ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} satisfies

𝖽⁡(ρ)⩽𝗐⁡(ρ)⋅(𝖽⁡(𝒞)+1).\mathsf{d}(\rho)\,\leqslant\,\mathsf{w}(\rho)\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C})+1).

If XX and YY are standard Borel spaces, we say that an (X,Y)(X,Y)-connection ρ\rho is Borel if ρ⁡(f):X⇀ℕ\rho(f)\colon X\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} is a Borel function whenever f:Y⇀ℕf\colon Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} is Borel. If ℬ\mathscr{B} and 𝒞\mathscr{C} are Borel CSPs and there is a Borel reduction ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C}, we say that ℬ\mathscr{B} is Borel-reducible to 𝒞\mathscr{C}.

It is clear that the (Borel-)reducibility relation is reflexive: the identity map [X⇀ℕ]→[X⇀ℕ][X\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}]\to[X\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}] is a reduction from any CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} on XX to itself (the width of this reduction is 11). It is not hard to see that this relation is also transitive. Indeed, we have the following:

Lemma 5.5 (Transitivity).

If ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} and σ:𝒞↝𝒟\sigma\colon\mathscr{C}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{D} are Borel reductions between Borel CSPs, then the composition ρ∘σ\rho\circ\sigma is a Borel reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to 𝒟\mathscr{D} such that

(5.6) 𝗐⁡(ρ∘σ)⩽𝗐⁡(ρ)​𝗐​(σ)and𝖽⁡(ρ∘σ)⩽𝗐⁡(ρ)​𝖽​(σ).\mathsf{w}(\rho\circ\sigma)\,\leqslant\,\mathsf{w}(\rho)\mathsf{w}(\sigma)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathsf{d}(\rho\circ\sigma)\,\leqslant\,\mathsf{w}(\rho)\mathsf{d}(\sigma).
Proof.

Let the given Borel CSPs ℬ\mathscr{B}, 𝒞\mathscr{C}, and 𝒟\mathscr{D} be on spaces XX, YY, and ZZ respectively. It is clear that ρ∘σ\rho\circ\sigma is a Borel (X,Z)(X,Z)-connection that sends solutions to 𝒟\mathscr{D} to solutions to ℬ\mathscr{B}. It remains to verify inequalities (5.6) (the first of which implies that ρ∘σ\rho\circ\sigma is local). To this end, notice that for any x∈Xx\in X, the union ⋃{Sσ​(y):y∈Sρ​(x)}\bigcup\{S_{\sigma}(y)\,:\,y\in S_{\rho}(x)\} (ρ∘σ)(\rho\circ\sigma)-determines xx, has size at most 𝗐⁡(ρ)​𝗐​(σ)\mathsf{w}(\rho)\mathsf{w}(\sigma), and intersects at most 𝗐⁡(ρ)​𝖽​(σ)\mathsf{w}(\rho)\mathsf{d}(\sigma) sets of the form dom⁡(D)\mathrm{dom}(D) for D∈𝒟D\in\mathscr{D}. ∎

5.C.  Partial solutions

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a CSP and let g:X⇀[m]g\colon X\rightharpoonup[m] be a partial function. We say that gg is a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} if gg can be extended to a solution f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m]. Given a partial map g:X⇀[m]g\colon X\rightharpoonup[m] and B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}, let B/gB/g be the constraint with domain dom⁡(B/g)≔dom⁡(B)∖dom⁡(g)\mathrm{dom}(B/g)\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(B)\setminus\mathrm{dom}(g) given by

B/g≔{φ:dom(B)∖dom(g)→[m]:φ∪(g|dom(B))∈B}.B/g\,\coloneqq\,\{\varphi\colon\mathrm{dom}(B)\setminus\mathrm{dom}(g)\to[m]\,:\,\varphi\cup({{g}|{\mathrm{dom}(B)}})\in B\}.

In other words, φ∈B/g\varphi\in B/g if and only if φ∪g\varphi\cup g violates the constraint BB. Note that if dom⁡(B)⊆dom⁡(g)\mathrm{dom}(B)\subseteq\mathrm{dom}(g), then dom⁡(B/g)=∅\mathrm{dom}(B/g)=\varnothing; specifically, B/g={∅}B/g=\{\varnothing\} if gg violates BB, and B/g=∅B/g=\varnothing otherwise. Let

ℬ/g≔{B/g:B∈ℬ}.\mathscr{B}/g\,\coloneqq\,\{B/g\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}.

We view ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g as a CSP on X∖dom⁡(g)X\setminus\mathrm{dom}(g). By construction, 𝖽⁡(ℬ/g)⩽𝖽⁡(ℬ)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}/g)\leqslant\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B}). If the CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} and the partial map gg are Borel, then the CSP ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g is Borel as well. The following observation is immediate:

Lemma 5.7.

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a CSP and let g:X⇀[m]g\colon X\rightharpoonup[m] be a partial function. Then gg is a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} if and only if ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g has a solution.

Proof.

If h:X∖dom⁡(g)→[m]h\colon X\setminus\mathrm{dom}(g)\to[m] is a solution to ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g, then g∪hg\cup h is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} extending gg. Conversely, if ff is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} extending gg, then f|(X∖dom⁡(g)){{f}|{(X\setminus\mathrm{dom}(g))}} is a solution to ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g. ∎

Next we notice that a countable union of partial solutions is also a partial solution:

Lemma 5.8.

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a CSP. If (gi)i=0∞(g_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} is a sequence such that for all i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, gig_{i} is a partial solution to ℬ/(g0∪…∪gi−1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i-1}), then ⋃i=0∞gi\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}g_{i} is a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}.

Proof.

It is clear that each finite union g0∪…∪gig_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i} is a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}, so let fi:X→[m]f_{i}\colon X\to[m] be a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} extending g0∪…∪gig_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i}. Consider the product space [m]X[m]^{X}, where the topology on [m][m] is discrete. By Tychonoff’s theorem, [m]X[m]^{X} is compact. The set 𝔖\mathfrak{S} of all solutions to ℬ\mathscr{B} is closed in [m]X[m]^{X}, and, for each i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, the set 𝔈i\mathfrak{E}_{i} of all f:X→[m]f\colon X\to[m] extending gig_{i} is also closed. The functions fif_{i}, i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, certify that the collection {𝔖}∪{𝔈i:i∈ℕ}\{\mathfrak{S}\}\cup\{\mathfrak{E}_{i}\,:\,i\in{\mathbb{N}}\} has the finite intersection property, so there is some f∈𝔖∩⋂{𝔈i:i∈ℕ}f\in\mathfrak{S}\cap\bigcap\{\mathfrak{E}_{i}\,:\,i\in{\mathbb{N}}\}. This ff is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} extending ⋃i=0∞gi\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}g_{i}, and we are done. ∎

Now we discuss the interplay between partial solutions and reductions:

Lemma 5.9.

Let ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} be a Borel reduction between Borel CSPs. If gg is a Borel partial solution to 𝒞\mathscr{C}, then ρ⁡(g)\rho(g) is a Borel partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} and ℬ/ρ⁡(g)\mathscr{B}/\rho(g) is Borel-reducible to 𝒞/g\mathscr{C}/g.

Proof.

Let the given Borel CSPs ℬ\mathscr{B} and 𝒞\mathscr{C} be on spaces XX and YY respectively. For brevity, set Y′≔dom⁡(g)Y^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(g) and X′≔dom⁡(ρ⁡(g))X^{\prime}\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(\rho(g)). The fact that ρ⁡(g)\rho(g) is Borel follows from the Borelness of ρ\rho. If ff is a solution to 𝒞\mathscr{C} extending gg, then ρ⁡(f)\rho(f) is a solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} and, since ρ\rho is monotone, ρ⁡(f)\rho(f) extends ρ⁡(g)\rho(g), proving that ρ⁡(g)\rho(g) is a partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}. Finally, the map

[Y∖Y′⇀ℕ]→[X∖X′⇀ℕ]:h↦ρ(g∪h)|(X∖X′)[Y\setminus Y^{\prime}\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}]\to[X\setminus X^{\prime}\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}]\colon h\mapsto{{\rho(g\cup h)}|{(X\setminus X^{\prime})}}

is a Borel reduction from ℬ/ρ⁡(g)\mathscr{B}/\rho(g) to 𝒞/g\mathscr{C}/g. ∎

5.D.  The LLL as a distributed problem

There are several natural and essentially equivalent ways of encoding a CSP as a local coloring problem on an auxiliary graph. For our purposes, the following formalism will be most convenient. A graph-CSP with range m∈ℕ+m\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} is a pair (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}), where GG is a graph and ℬ:V(G)→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon V(G)\to^{?}[m] is a bounded CSP on V⁡(G)V(G) such that 𝖽⁡(ℬ)<∞\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})<\infty, with the following property: If xx, y∈V⁡(G)y\in V(G) are distinct vertices such that xx, y∈dom⁡(B)y\in\mathrm{dom}(B) for some B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B}, then xx and yy are adjacent in GG. A graph-CSP (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) can be naturally interpreted as a structured graph, where, for each tuple of vertices (x1,…,xk)∈V​(G)<∞(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V(G)^{<\infty}, the structure contains the information about all the constraints B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} such that dom⁡(B)={x1,…,xk}\mathrm{dom}(B)=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}. Formally, we construct a structure map σ\sigma on GG as follows. A tuple 𝒙=(x1,…,xk)∈V​(G)<∞\bm{x}=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{k})\in V(G)^{<\infty} is in the domain of σ\sigma if and only if:

  • —

    the vertices x1x_{1}, …, xkx_{k} are pairwise distinct; and

  • —

    there is a constraint B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} with dom⁡(B)={x1,…,xk}\mathrm{dom}(B)=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}.

To compute σ⁡(𝒙)\sigma(\bm{x}) for 𝒙∈dom⁡(σ)\bm{x}\in\mathrm{dom}(\sigma), let ι:{x1,…,xk}→[k]\iota\colon\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\to[k] be given by ι⁡(xi)≔i\iota(x_{i})\coloneqq i. For each B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} with dom⁡(B)={x1,…,xk}\mathrm{dom}(B)=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}, let B∗B^{\ast} be the set of all maps φ:[k]→[m]\varphi\colon[k]\to[m] such that φ∘ι∈B\varphi\circ\iota\in B, and let

σ⁡(𝒙)≔{B∗:B∈ℬ​ and ​dom​(B)={x1,…,xk}}.\sigma(\bm{x})\,\coloneqq\,\{B^{\ast}\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\text{ and }\mathrm{dom}(B)=\{x_{1},\ldots,x_{k}\}\}.

Since ℬ\mathscr{B} is bounded, σ\sigma is defined on tuples of bounded length. Furthermore, since 𝖽⁡(ℬ)<∞\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})<\infty, the set σ⁡(𝒙)\sigma(\bm{x}) is finite for every 𝒙\bm{x}, which means that the range of σ\sigma is contained in the countable set [[[ℕ⇀ℕ]<∞]<∞]<∞[[[{\mathbb{N}}\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}]^{<\infty}]^{<\infty}]^{<\infty}. As explained after Definition 2.1, this means that we can indeed view σ\sigma as a structure map on GG. We then identify (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) with the structured graph (G,σ,m)(G,\sigma,m). (Here mm is interpreted as a global parameter “known” to every vertex; this can be realized, formally, by viewing it as a function V⁡(G)→ℕV(G)\to{\mathbb{N}} mapping each vertex x∈V⁡(G)x\in V(G) to mm.)

Let (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) be a graph-CSP. The requirement that xx and yy are adjacent whenever xx, y∈dom⁡(B)y\in\mathrm{dom}(B) for some B∈ℬB\in\mathscr{B} means that in one round of the 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} model, each vertex can “learn” about all constraints that involve it. Because of this, the problem of solving ℬ\mathscr{B} can be naturally encoded as a local coloring problem ΠCSP=(1,𝒫CSP)\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP}}=(1,\mathcal{P}_{\mathrm{CSP}}). Given parameters mm, kk, pp, and dd, let 𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(m,k,p,d)\mathsf{CSP}(m,k,p,d) denote the set of all isomorphism types of finite graph-CSPs (G,ℬ)(G,\mathscr{B}) such that:

  • —

    the range of ℬ\mathscr{B} is mm;

  • —

    sup{|dom⁡(B)|:B∈ℬ}⩽k\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(B)|\,:\,B\in\mathscr{B}\}\leqslant k;

  • —

    𝗉⁡(ℬ)⩽p\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant p and 𝖽⁡(ℬ)⩽d\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})\leqslant d.

We shall need the following bound on the randomized 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} complexity of solving graph-CSPs:

Theorem 5.10 (Ghaffari–Harris–Kuhn [GHK18]).

If mm, kk, pp, and dd satisfy p​(d+1)8⩽2−15p(d+1)^{8}\leqslant 2^{-15}, then

𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽ΠCSP,𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(m,k,p,d)​(n)=exp⁡(O⁡(log⁡log⁡n))=o⁡(log⁡n).\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP}},\mathsf{CSP}(m,k,p,d)}(n)\,=\,\exp(O(\sqrt{\log\log n}))\,=\,o(\log n).

(Here the implicit constants in the asymptotic notation may depend on mm, kk, and dd.)

We say that a bounded CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is an (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP if 𝗉⁡(ℬ)​(𝖽⁡(ℬ)+1)N⩽ε\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{B})(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{B})+1)^{N}\leqslant\varepsilon. A bounded Borel CSP ℬ\mathscr{B} is a potential Borel (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP if it is Borel-reducible to a Borel (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP. Using Theorem 5.10, we derive the following “bootstrapping lemma,” inspired by [FG17, §3.2]:

Lemma 5.11 (Bootstrapping).

Let ℬ\mathscr{B} be a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP. Then ℬ\mathscr{B} is in fact a potential Borel (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP for any N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0. Moreover, there exist a Borel (N,ε)(N,\varepsilon)-CSP 𝒞\mathscr{C} and a Borel reduction ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} such that 𝗉⁡(𝒞)​𝖽​(ρ)N⩽ε\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})\mathsf{d}(\rho)^{N}\leqslant\varepsilon.

Proof.

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be the given Borel CSP and let σ:ℬ↝𝒟\sigma\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{D} be a Borel reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to a Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP 𝒟:Y→?[ℓ]\mathscr{D}\colon Y\to^{?}[\ell]. Set k≔sup{|dom⁡(D)|:D∈𝒟}k\coloneqq\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(D)|\,:\,D\in\mathscr{D}\}, p≔𝗉⁡(𝒟)p\coloneqq\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{D}), and d≔𝖽⁡(𝒟)d\coloneqq\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{D}). Define a graph GG with V⁡(G)≔YV(G)\coloneqq Y by making distinct vertices xx and yy adjacent if and only if xx, y∈dom⁡(D)y\in\mathrm{dom}(D) for some D∈𝒟D\in\mathscr{D}. Then 𝑮≔(G,𝒟)\bm{G}\coloneqq(G,\mathscr{D}) is a graph-CSP. It is routine to check that, as a structured graph, 𝑮\bm{G} is Borel. Note that Δ≔Δ⁡(𝑮)=Δ⁡(G)⩽(k−1)​(d+1)\Delta\coloneqq\Delta(\bm{G})=\Delta(G)\leqslant(k-1)(d+1); in particular, Δ\Delta is finite. Consider the local coloring problem ΠCSP\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP}}. For n∈ℕ+n\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+}, let

T⁡(n)≔𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽ΠCSP,𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(ℓ,k,p,d)​(n)andR⁡(n)≔T⁡(n)+1.T(n)\,\coloneqq\,\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP}},\mathsf{CSP}(\ell,k,p,d)}(n)\qquad\text{and}\qquad R(n)\,\coloneqq\,T(n)+1.

By Theorem 5.10, T⁡(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)T(n)=o(\log n), and hence R⁡(n)=o⁡(log⁡n)R(n)=o(\log n). Let mn∈ℕ+m_{n}\in{\mathbb{N}}^{+} and a 𝖫𝖮𝖢𝖠𝖫\mathsf{LOCAL} algorithm 𝒜n\mathcal{A}_{n} witness the bound 𝖱𝖺𝗇𝖽ΠCSP,𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(ℓ,k,p,d)​(n)⩽T⁡(n)\mathsf{Rand}_{\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP}},\mathsf{CSP}(\ell,k,p,d)}(n)\leqslant T(n). For all large enough nn, 𝑮\bm{G} is (R⁡(n),n)(R(n),n)-locally in 𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(ℓ,k,p,d)\mathsf{CSP}(\ell,k,p,d). Indeed, the class 𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(ℓ,k,p,d)\mathsf{CSP}(\ell,k,p,d) is closed under adding isolated vertices, and every finite induced subgraph of 𝑮\bm{G} is in 𝖢𝖲𝖯⁡(ℓ,k,p,d)\mathsf{CSP}(\ell,k,p,d). Thus, we only need to verify that, for large nn, |B𝑮​(x,R⁡(n))|⩽n|B_{\bm{G}}(x,R(n))|\leqslant n for all x∈Yx\in Y, which holds as

|B𝑮​(x,R⁡(n))|⩽ 1+Δo⁡(log⁡n)=no⁡(1).|B_{\bm{G}}(x,R(n))|\,\leqslant\,1+\Delta^{o(\log n)}\,=\,n^{o(1)}.

By Lemma 4.6, for every large enough nn, there is a bounded Borel CSP 𝒞n:Y→?[mn]\mathscr{C}_{n}\colon Y\to^{?}[m_{n}] such that:

  1. (i)

    for every solution ϑ:Y→[mn]\vartheta\colon Y\to[m_{n}] to 𝒞n\mathscr{C}_{n}, the function 𝒜n​(𝑮ϑ,T⁡(n))\mathcal{A}_{n}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T(n)) is a ΠCSP\Pi_{\mathrm{CSP}}-coloring of 𝑮\bm{G}, or, equivalently, a solution to 𝒟\mathscr{D};

  2. (ii)

    𝗉⁡(𝒞n)⩽1/n\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}_{n})\leqslant 1/n and 𝖽⁡(𝒞n)⩽sup{|B𝑮​(x,2​R​(n))|−1:x∈Y}⩽1+Δo⁡(log⁡n)=no⁡(1)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}_{n})\leqslant\sup\{|B_{\bm{G}}(x,2R(n))|-1\,:\,x\in Y\}\leqslant 1+\Delta^{o(\log n)}=n^{o(1)}.

Using (i), we can define a Borel reduction τn:𝒟↝𝒞n\tau_{n}\colon\mathscr{D}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C}_{n} by setting, for all ϑ:Y⇀ℕ\vartheta\colon Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} and x∈Yx\in Y,

τ⁡(ϑ)​(x)≔{𝒜n​(𝑮ϑ,T⁡(n))​(x)if V⁡(B𝑮​(x,R⁡(n)))⊆dom⁡(ϑ);undefinedotherwise.\tau(\vartheta)(x)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\mathcal{A}_{n}(\bm{G}_{\vartheta},T(n))(x)&\text{if $V(B_{\bm{G}}(x,R(n)))\subseteq\mathrm{dom}(\vartheta)$};\\ \text{undefined}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

Each x∈Yx\in Y is τn\tau_{n}-determined by the vertex set of the radius-R⁡(n)R(n) ball around xx in 𝑮\bm{G}. Thus,

𝗐⁡(τn)⩽sup{|B𝑮​(x,R⁡(n))|:x∈Y}⩽ 1+Δo⁡(log⁡n)=no⁡(1),\mathsf{w}(\tau_{n})\,\leqslant\,\sup\{|B_{\bm{G}}(x,R(n))|\,:\,x\in Y\}\,\leqslant\,1+\Delta^{o(\log n)}\,=\,n^{o(1)},

and hence 𝖽⁡(τn)⩽𝗐⁡(τn)​(𝖽⁡(𝒞n)+1)⩽no⁡(1)\mathsf{d}(\tau_{n})\leqslant\mathsf{w}(\tau_{n})(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}_{n})+1)\leqslant n^{o(1)} as well. By Lemma 5.5, ρn≔σ∘τn\rho_{n}\coloneqq\sigma\circ\tau_{n} is a Borel reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to 𝒞n\mathscr{C}_{n} such that 𝖽⁡(ρn)⩽𝗐⁡(σ)​𝖽​(τn)⩽no⁡(1)\mathsf{d}(\rho_{n})\leqslant\mathsf{w}(\sigma)\mathsf{d}(\tau_{n})\leqslant n^{o(1)} (since 𝗐⁡(σ)\mathsf{w}(\sigma) is a constant independent of nn). Now fix N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and ε>0\varepsilon>0. For sufficiently large nn, we can write

𝗉⁡(𝒞n)⋅(𝖽⁡(𝒞n)+1)N⩽1n⋅(no⁡(1))N=n−1+o⁡(1)<ε,\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}_{n})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}_{n})+1)^{N}\,\leqslant\,\frac{1}{n}\cdot(n^{o(1)})^{N}\,=\,n^{-1+o(1)}\,<\,\varepsilon,

and similarly 𝗉⁡(𝒞n)​𝖽​(ρn)N<ε\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}_{n})\mathsf{d}(\rho_{n})^{N}<\varepsilon. Therefore, for all sufficiently large nn, the CSP 𝒞≔𝒞n\mathscr{C}\coloneqq\mathscr{C}_{n} and the reduction ρ≔ρn\rho\coloneqq\rho_{n} are as desired. ∎

5.E.  Proof of Theorem 2.20(i)

In order to build partial solutions to CSPs, we use the following lemma, which is an adaptation of [FG17, Lemma 8] to the measurable setting:

Lemma 5.12 (Partial solutions).

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a Borel CSP and let ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} be a Borel reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to a Borel CSP 𝒞:Y→?[n]\mathscr{C}\colon Y\to^{?}[n]. Assume that 𝒞\mathscr{C} is a (2,e−2/n2)(2,e^{-2}/n^{2})-CSP. If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on XX, then there is a Borel partial solution h:Y⇀[n]h\colon Y\rightharpoonup[n] to 𝒞\mathscr{C} such that

𝗉⁡(𝒞/h)⩽n​𝗉⁡(𝒞)andμ⁡(dom⁡(ρ⁡(h)))⩾ 1−𝖽⁡(ρ)​𝗉⁡(𝒞).\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}/h)\,\leqslant\,n\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mu(\mathrm{dom}(\rho(h)))\,\geqslant\,1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}.

For a set AA and i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}, let 𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(A,i)\mathsf{const}(A,i) denote the constant function on AA sending every x∈Ax\in A to ii. An important observation is that if CC is a (Y,n)(Y,n)-constraint and A⊆YA\subseteq Y is a subset such that |A∩dom⁡(C)|⩽1|A\cap\mathrm{dom}(C)|\leqslant 1, then

(5.13) ℙ⁡[C]=1n​∑i=1nℙ⁡[C/𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(A,i)].\mathbb{P}[C]\,=\,\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\mathbb{P}[C/\mathsf{const}(A,i)].

Indeed, if A∩dom⁡(C)=∅A\cap\mathrm{dom}(C)=\varnothing, then C/𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(A,i)=CC/\mathsf{const}(A,i)=C for all i∈[n]i\in[n] and (5.13) is trivial. Otherwise, there is a single element x∈A∩dom⁡(C)x\in A\cap\mathrm{dom}(C), and ℙ⁡[C/𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍⁡(A,i)]\mathbb{P}[C/\mathsf{const}(A,i)] is the probability that a uniformly random function φ:dom⁡(C)→[n]\varphi\colon\mathrm{dom}(C)\to[n] is in CC conditioned on the event φ⁡(x)=i\varphi(x)=i. Since each of these events has probability 1/n1/n, equation (5.13) follows.

We say that a subset A⊆XA\subseteq X is 𝒞\mathscr{C}-discrete if |A∩dom⁡(C)|⩽1|A\cap\mathrm{dom}(C)|\leqslant 1 for all C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C}. The first step in the construction of a desired partial solution hh is to fix a partition Y=A1⊔…⊔ANY=A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{N} of YY into finitely many Borel 𝒞\mathscr{C}-discrete sets. To see that such a partition exists, let GG be the graph with vertex set YY in which distinct vertices xx and yy adjacent if and only if xx, y∈dom⁡(C)y\in\mathrm{dom}(C) for some C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C}. Since 𝒞\mathscr{C} is bounded and d<∞d<\infty, GG has finite maximum degree, so, by Theorem 3.1, GG admits a Borel proper coloring c:Y→[N]c\colon Y\to[N] for some N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}}. Letting Ak≔c−1​(k)A_{k}\coloneqq c^{-1}(k), the partition Y=A1⊔…⊔ANY=A_{1}\sqcup\ldots\sqcup A_{N} is as desired. Next, we need the following definition:

Definition 5.12.1 (Dangerous constraints and elements).

Given a partial map h:Y⇀[n]h\colon Y\rightharpoonup[n], we say that a constraint C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C} is hh-dangerous if ℙ⁡[C/h]>p\mathbb{P}[C/h]>\sqrt{p}, and an element x∈Yx\in Y is hh-dangerous if x∈dom⁡(C)x\in\mathrm{dom}(C) for some hh-dangerous constraint C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C}. We use ⌢ to denote concatenation of finite sequences and write u⊑wu\sqsubseteq w to mean that a sequence uu is an initial segment of a sequence ww. hu⌢i≔hu⊔𝖼𝗈𝗇𝗌𝗍(Ak∖D(hu),i).h_{u{{}^{\smallfrown}}i}\,\coloneqq\,h_{u}\sqcup\mathsf{const}(A_{k}\setminus D(h_{u}),i).

Claim 5.12.3.

Using Claim .2 and the fact that 𝒞\mathscr{C} is a (2,e−2/n2)(2,e^{-2}/n^{2})-CSP, we can write

In view of Claims .2 and .3, it only remains to argue that there is some w∈[n]Nw\in[n]^{N} such that μ⁡(dom⁡(ρ⁡(hw)))⩾1−𝖽⁡(ρ)​p\mu(\mathrm{dom}(\rho(h_{w})))\geqslant 1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{p}.
