(5.16) ⩾ 1−∑Cℙw​[C is w-dangerous]⩾ 1−𝖽⁡(ρ)​p,\displaystyle\geqslant\,1-\sum_{C}\mathbb{P}_{w}[\text{$C$ is $w$-dangerous}]\,\geqslant\,1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{p},

where the sum is over all C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C} such that dom⁡(C)∩Sρ​(x)≠∅\mathrm{dom}(C)\cap S_{\rho}(x)\neq\varnothing. Since (5.16) holds for every x∈Xx\in X, we conclude that, by Fubini’s theorem, there is a choice of w∈[n]Nw\in[n]^{N} such that μ⁡(dom⁡(ρ⁡(hw)))⩾1−𝖽⁡(ρ)​p\mu(\mathrm{dom}(\rho(h_{w})))\geqslant 1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{p}, and the proof is complete ∎

The upper bound on 𝗉⁡(𝒞/g)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}/g) given by Lemma 5.12 depends on nn, the cardinality of the range of 𝒞\mathscr{C}. In order to control it, we show that every bounded CSP is reducible to a binary CSP, i.e., one with range [2][2]:

Lemma 5.17.

Let ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} be a Borel reduction between bounded Borel CSPs and let ε>0\varepsilon>0. Then there exist a bounded binary Borel CSP 𝒟\mathscr{D} and a Borel reduction σ:ℬ↝𝒟\sigma\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{D} such that

𝗉(𝒟)⩽(1+ε)𝗉(𝒞),𝖽(𝒟)=𝖽(𝒞),and𝖽(σ)=𝖽(ρ).\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{D})\,\leqslant\,(1+\varepsilon)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}),\qquad\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{D})\,=\,\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}),\qquad\text{and}\qquad\mathsf{d}(\sigma)\,=\,\mathsf{d}(\rho).
Proof.

Let the given Borel CSPs be ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] and 𝒞:Y→?[n]\mathscr{C}\colon Y\to^{?}[n]. We need to somehow reduce nn to just 22. The idea is to represent each i∈[n]i\in[n] by a binary sequence of an appropriate finite length NN. We can then replace every element y∈Yy\in Y by NN copies (y,1)(y,1), …, (y,N)(y,N) and identify a solution f:Y→[n]f\colon Y\to[n] to 𝒞\mathscr{C} with a function f′:Y×[N]→[2]f^{\prime}\colon Y\times[N]\to[2] where f′​(y,i)f^{\prime}(y,i) is the ii-th digit in a binary representation of f⁡(y)f(y). This will allow us to reduce 𝒞\mathscr{C} to a CSP 𝒟:Y×[N]→?[2]\mathscr{D}\colon Y\times[N]\to^{?}[2]. We remark that slight technical complications arise from the fact that nn may not be a power of 2 (this is why we lose a factor of 1+ε1+\varepsilon in the bound on 𝗉⁡(𝒟)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{D})).

Let us now describe the construction formally. Since the CSP 𝒞\mathscr{C} is bounded by assumption, the value k≔sup{|dom⁡(C)|:C∈𝒞}k\coloneqq\sup\{|\mathrm{dom}(C)|\,:\,C\in\mathscr{C}\} is finite. Fix δ>0\delta>0 such that (1+δ)k⩽1+ε(1+\delta)^{k}\leqslant 1+\varepsilon. Let N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} be so large that it is possible to express 2N2^{N} as a sum of the form 2N=s1+s2+⋯+sn2^{N}=s_{1}+s_{2}+\cdots+s_{n}, where each sis_{i} is a positive integer and max⁡{si:i∈[n]}⩽(1+δ)​2N/n\max\{s_{i}\,:\,i\in[n]\}\leqslant(1+\delta)2^{N}/n (so 2N2^{N} is “approximately divisible by nn”). Fix an arbitrary mapping ξ:[2]N→[n]\xi\colon[2]^{N}\to[n] such that |ξ−1​(i)|=si|\xi^{-1}(i)|=s_{i} for each i∈[n]i\in[n]. We think of each tuple (c1,…,cN)∈[2]N(c_{1},\ldots,c_{N})\in[2]^{N} as a “binary code” representing the value ξ⁡(c1,…,cN)∈[n]\xi(c_{1},\ldots,c_{N})\in[n].

Let Z≔Y×[N]Z\coloneqq Y\times[N] and for each f:Z⇀ℕf\colon Z\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}}, define τ⁡(f):Y⇀ℕ\tau(f)\colon Y\rightharpoonup{\mathbb{N}} as follows:

τ⁡(f)​(y)≔{ξ⁡(f⁡(y,1),…,f⁡(y,N))if (y,i)∈dom⁡(f) and f⁡(y,i)∈[2] for all i∈[N];undefinedotherwise.\tau(f)(y)\,\coloneqq\,\begin{cases}\xi(f(y,1),\ldots,f(y,N))&\text{if $(y,i)\in\mathrm{dom}(f)$ and $f(y,i)\in[2]$ for all $i\in[N]$};\\ \text{undefined}&\text{otherwise}.\end{cases}

It is clear that τ\tau is a Borel (Y,Z)(Y,Z)-connection such that 𝗐⁡(τ)=N\mathsf{w}(\tau)=N, with the set {(y,1),…,(y,N)}\{(y,1),\ldots,(y,N)\} τ\tau-determining each y∈Yy\in Y. Next we define a binary Borel CSP 𝒟\mathscr{D} on ZZ so that τ\tau is a reduction from 𝒞\mathscr{C} to 𝒟\mathscr{D}, in the obvious way. Namely, for each C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C}, we let C∗C^{\ast} be the (Z,2)(Z,2)-constraint with dom⁡(C∗)≔dom⁡(C)×[N]\mathrm{dom}(C^{\ast})\coloneqq\mathrm{dom}(C)\times[N] given by C∗≔{φ:dom(C)×[N]→[2]:τ(φ)∈C}C^{\ast}\coloneqq\{\varphi\colon\mathrm{dom}(C)\times[N]\to[2]\,:\,\tau(\varphi)\in C\}, and set 𝒟≔{C∗:C∈𝒞}\mathscr{D}\coloneqq\{C^{\ast}\,:\,C\in\mathscr{C}\}. Let σ≔ρ∘τ\sigma\coloneqq\rho\circ\tau. By Lemma 5.5, σ\sigma is a Borel reduction from ℬ\mathscr{B} to 𝒟\mathscr{D}. We claim that the CSP 𝒟\mathscr{D} and the reduction σ\sigma are as desired.

The equality 𝖽⁡(𝒟)=𝖽⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{D})=\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}) follows since for all C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C}, |N⁡(C∗)|=|N⁡(C)||\mathrm{N}(C^{\ast})|=|\mathrm{N}(C)|. To see that 𝖽⁡(σ)=𝖽⁡(ρ)\mathsf{d}(\sigma)=\mathsf{d}(\rho), observe that for each x∈Xx\in X, the set Sρ​(x)×[N]S_{\rho}(x)\times[N] σ\sigma-determines xx and dom⁡(C∗)∩(Sρ​(x)×[N])≠∅\mathrm{dom}(C^{\ast})\cap(S_{\rho}(x)\times[N])\neq\varnothing if and only if dom⁡(C)∩Sρ​(x)≠∅\mathrm{dom}(C)\cap S_{\rho}(x)\neq\varnothing. Finally, to bound 𝗉⁡(𝒟)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{D}), let C∈𝒞C\in\mathscr{C} and consider an arbitrary function ψ∈C\psi\in C. If φ:dom⁡(C∗)→[2]\varphi\colon\mathrm{dom}(C^{\ast})\to[2] satisfies τ⁡(φ)=ψ\tau(\varphi)=\psi, then (φ⁡(y,1),…,φ⁡(y,N))∈ξ−1​(ψ⁡(y))(\varphi(y,1),\ldots,\varphi(y,N))\in\xi^{-1}(\psi(y)) for all y∈dom⁡(C)y\in\mathrm{dom}(C). Hence there are at most (1+δ)​2N/n(1+\delta)2^{N}/n possible values for the tuple (φ⁡(y,1),…,φ⁡(y,N))(\varphi(y,1),\ldots,\varphi(y,N)), and so the number of such functions φ\varphi cannot exceed ((1+δ)​2N/n)|dom⁡(C)|((1+\delta)2^{N}/n)^{|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}. Therefore,

ℙ⁡[C∗]=|C∗|2|dom⁡(C∗)|\displaystyle\mathbb{P}[C^{\ast}]\,=\,\frac{|C^{\ast}|}{2^{|\mathrm{dom}(C^{\ast})|}}\, =∑ψ∈C|{φ:τ⁡(φ)=ψ}|2N​|dom⁡(C)|⩽12N​|dom⁡(C)|⋅|C|⋅((1+δ)​2Nn)|dom⁡(C)|\displaystyle=\,\frac{\sum_{\psi\in C}|\{\varphi\,:\,\tau(\varphi)=\psi\}|}{2^{N|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}}\,\leqslant\,\frac{1}{2^{N|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}}\cdot|C|\cdot\left(\frac{(1+\delta)2^{N}}{n}\right)^{|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}
=(1+δ)|dom⁡(C)|⋅|C|n|dom⁡(C)|=(1+δ)|dom⁡(C)|​ℙ​[C]⩽(1+ε)​ℙ​[C],\displaystyle=\,(1+\delta)^{|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}\cdot\frac{|C|}{n^{|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}}\,=\,(1+\delta)^{|\mathrm{dom}(C)|}\mathbb{P}[C]\,\leqslant\,(1+\varepsilon)\mathbb{P}[C],

and thus 𝗉⁡(𝒟)⩽(1+ε)​𝗉​(𝒞)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{D})\leqslant(1+\varepsilon)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}), as desired. ∎

Now we can combine Lemmas 5.11, 5.12, and 5.17 to obtain the following:

Lemma 5.18.

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP. If μ\mu is a probability Borel measure on XX, then ℬ\mathscr{B} admits a Borel partial solution g:X⇀[m]g\colon X\rightharpoonup[m] such that μ⁡(dom⁡(g))⩾1/2\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g))\geqslant 1/2 and ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g is again a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP.

Proof.

Using Lemmas 5.11 and 5.17, we can find a binary Borel (16,2−32)(16,2^{-32})-CSP 𝒞\mathscr{C} and a Borel reduction ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} such that 𝗉⁡(𝒞)​𝖽​(ρ)2⩽1/4\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})\mathsf{d}(\rho)^{2}\leqslant 1/4. Let hh be a partial Borel solution to 𝒞\mathscr{C} satisfying the conclusion of Lemma 5.12 and define g≔ρ⁡(h)g\coloneqq\rho(h). By Lemma 5.9, gg is a Borel partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} and ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g is Borel-reducible to 𝒞/h\mathscr{C}/h. Thus, it suffices to verify that μ⁡(dom⁡(g))⩾1/2\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g))\geqslant 1/2 and 𝒞/h\mathscr{C}/h is an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP. By the choice of hh, we have

μ⁡(dom⁡(g))⩾ 1−𝖽⁡(ρ)​𝗉⁡(𝒞)⩾ 1−1/2= 1/2,\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g))\,\geqslant\,1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}\,\geqslant\,1-1/2\,=\,1/2,

as desired. Furthermore,

𝗉⁡(𝒞/h)⋅(𝖽⁡(𝒞/h)+1)8⩽ 2​𝗉⁡(𝒞)⋅(𝖽⁡(𝒞)+1)8⩽ 2⋅2−32= 2−15.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}/h)\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}/h)+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2\cdot\sqrt{2^{-32}}\,=\,2^{-15}.

Thus, 𝒞/h\mathscr{C}/h is indeed an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP, and we are done. ∎

With Lemma 5.18 in hand, it is easy to finish the proof of Theorem 2.20(i). Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP and let μ\mu be a probability Borel measure on XX. Repeated applications of Lemma 5.18 produce a sequence (gi)i=0∞(g_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} such that for all i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}:

  • —

    ℬ/(g0∪…∪gi−1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i-1}) is a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP;

  • —

    gig_{i} is a Borel partial solution to ℬ/(g0∪…∪gi−1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i-1}); and

  • —

    μ⁡(dom⁡(gi))⩾(1−μ⁡(dom⁡(g0))−⋯−μ⁡(dom⁡(gi−1)))/2\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g_{i}))\geqslant(1-\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g_{0}))-\cdots-\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g_{i-1})))/2.

Let g≔⋃i=0∞gig\coloneqq\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}g_{i}. Then μ⁡(dom⁡(g))=1\mu(\mathrm{dom}(g))=1. By Lemma 5.8, gg is a Borel partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}, so let ff be any solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} extending gg. Since ff agrees with the Borel function gg on a μ\mu-conull set, ff is μ\mu-measurable, and the proof is complete.

5.F.  Proof of Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C(ii)

In the Baire category setting, instead of Lemma 5.18 we use the following:

Lemma 5.19.

Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP. Then there is a finite set 𝒢\mathcal{G} of Borel partial solutions to ℬ\mathscr{B} such that:

  • —

    ⋃{dom⁡(g):g∈𝒢}=X\bigcup\{\mathrm{dom}(g)\,:\,g\in\mathcal{G}\}=X; and

  • —

    for every g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G}, ℬ/g\mathscr{B}/g is a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP.

Proof.

Using Lemmas 5.11 and 5.17, we can find a binary Borel (16,2−32)(16,2^{-32})-CSP 𝒞\mathscr{C} and a Borel reduction ρ:ℬ↝𝒞\rho\colon\mathscr{B}\rightsquigarrow\mathscr{C} such that 𝗉⁡(𝒞)​𝖽​(ρ)2⩽1/4\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})\mathsf{d}(\rho)^{2}\leqslant 1/4. Using the construction from the proof of Lemma 5.12, we obtain a natural number N∈ℕN\in{\mathbb{N}} and an assignment to each sequence w∈[2]Nw\in[2]^{N} of a Borel partial solution hwh_{w} to 𝒞\mathscr{C} with the following properties:

  1. (i)

    for all w∈[2]Nw\in[2]^{N}, 𝗉⁡(𝒞/hw)⩽2​𝗉⁡(𝒞)\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}/h_{w})\leqslant 2\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})} (Claim .2); and

  2. (ii)

    for every x∈Xx\in X, ℙw[x∈dom(ρ(hw))]⩾1−𝖽(ρ)𝗉⁡(𝒞)\mathbb{P}_{w}[x\in\mathrm{dom}(\rho(h_{w}))]\geqslant 1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}, where ℙw\mathbb{P}_{w} denotes probability with respect to a uniformly random choice of w∈[2]Nw\in[2]^{N} (equation (5.16)).

From (i) it follows that each 𝒞/hw\mathscr{C}/h_{w} is an (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP, since

𝗉⁡(𝒞/hw)⋅(𝖽⁡(𝒞/hw)+1)8⩽ 2​𝗉⁡(𝒞)⋅(𝖽⁡(𝒞)+1)8⩽ 2⋅2−32= 2−15.\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C}/h_{w})\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C}/h_{w})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}\cdot(\mathsf{d}(\mathscr{C})+1)^{8}\,\leqslant\,2\cdot\sqrt{2^{-32}}\,=\,2^{-15}.

Furthermore, from (ii) it follows that for all x∈Xx\in X,

ℙw[x∈dom(ρ(hw))]⩾ 1−𝖽(ρ)𝗉⁡(𝒞)⩾ 1−1/2= 1/2.\mathbb{P}_{w}[x\in\mathrm{dom}(\rho(h_{w}))]\,\geqslant\,1-\mathsf{d}(\rho)\sqrt{\mathsf{p}(\mathscr{C})}\,\geqslant\,1-1/2\,=\,1/2.

In particular, for each x∈Xx\in X, there is some w∈[2]Nw\in[2]^{N} such that x∈dom⁡(ρ⁡(hw))x\in\mathrm{dom}(\rho(h_{w})). By Lemma 5.9, each ρ⁡(hw)\rho(h_{w}) is a Borel partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} and ℬ/ρ⁡(hw)\mathscr{B}/\rho(h_{w}) is Borel-reducible to 𝒞/hw\mathscr{C}/h_{w}. Therefore, the set 𝒢≔{ρ⁡(hw):w∈[2]N}\mathcal{G}\coloneqq\{\rho(h_{w})\,:\,w\in[2]^{N}\} is as desired. ∎

We are now ready to prove Theorem ′ ‣ 4.C(ii). Let ℬ:X→?[m]\mathscr{B}\colon X\to^{?}[m] be a Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP and let 𝒯\mathcal{T} be a countable set of compatible Polish topologies on XX. For each τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, fix a countable base 𝒰τ\mathcal{U}_{\tau} consisting of nonempty open sets, and let (τi,Ui)i=0∞(\tau_{i},U_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} be an enumeration of all pairs (τ,U)(\tau,U) with τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T} and U∈𝒰τU\in\mathcal{U}_{\tau}. Using Lemma 5.19, we can recursively build a sequence (gi)i=0∞(g_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} such that for all i∈ℕi\in{\mathbb{N}}:

  • —

    ℬ/(g0∪…∪gi−1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i-1}) is a potential Borel (8,2−15)(8,2^{-15})-CSP;

  • —

    gig_{i} is a Borel partial solution to ℬ/(g0∪…∪gi−1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i-1}); and

  • —

    the set (dom⁡(g0)∪…∪dom⁡(gi))∩Ui(\mathrm{dom}(g_{0})\cup\ldots\cup\mathrm{dom}(g_{i}))\cap U_{i} is τi\tau_{i}-nonmeager.

Specifically, once g0g_{0}, …, gi−1g_{i-1} have been constructed, we define gig_{i} as follows. Let 𝒢\mathcal{G} be a finite set of Borel partial solutions to ℬ/(g0∪…∪gi−1)\mathscr{B}/(g_{0}\cup\ldots\cup g_{i-1}) given by Lemma 5.19. Then

Ui⊆dom⁡(g0)∪…∪dom⁡(gi−1)∪⋃{dom⁡(g):g∈𝒢}.U_{i}\,\subseteq\,\mathrm{dom}(g_{0})\cup\ldots\cup\mathrm{dom}(g_{i-1})\cup\bigcup\{\mathrm{dom}(g)\,:\,g\in\mathcal{G}\}.

Since UiU_{i} is nonempty and τi\tau_{i}-open, it is τi\tau_{i}-nonmeager, so dom⁡(g)∩Ui\mathrm{dom}(g)\cap U_{i} must be τi\tau_{i}-nonmeager for some g∈{g0,…,gi−1}∪𝒢g\in\{g_{0},\ldots,g_{i-1}\}\cup\mathcal{G}. If dom⁡(gj)∩Ui\mathrm{dom}(g_{j})\cap U_{i} is τi\tau_{i}-nonmeager for some 0⩽j⩽i−10\leqslant j\leqslant i-1, then we can let gi≔∅g_{i}\coloneqq\varnothing, and otherwise we can make gig_{i} be any g∈𝒢g\in\mathcal{G} such that dom⁡(g)∩Ui\mathrm{dom}(g)\cap U_{i} is τi\tau_{i}-nonmeager.

Once we have built a sequence (gi)i=0∞(g_{i})_{i=0}^{\infty} as above, we let g≔⋃i=0∞gig\coloneqq\bigcup_{i=0}^{\infty}g_{i}. By Lemma 5.8, gg is a Borel partial solution to ℬ\mathscr{B}. Furthermore, for each τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, the set dom⁡(g)∩U\mathrm{dom}(g)\cap U is τ\tau-nonmeager for every U∈𝒰τU\in\mathcal{U}_{\tau}, which, by [Kec95, Proposition 8.26], implies that dom⁡(g)\mathrm{dom}(g) is τ\tau-comeager. Now let ff be any solution to ℬ\mathscr{B} extending gg. For each τ∈𝒯\tau\in\mathcal{T}, ff agrees with the Borel function gg on a τ\tau-comeager set, and therefore ff is τ\tau-Baire-measurable, which finishes the proof.
